text: Summary A chatbot can only answer as well as the store and product data behind it. Fix the foundation first, then add the answer layer. ChatSKU is that answer layer. It turns your existing catalog into a 24/7 buying assistant that answers product questions, builds quotes and captures orders. Virtina builds and fixes the store underneath it , with more than 14 years of B2B eCommerce work behind that. This guide shows what silent exits can cost, five checks you can run this week, and a 30-day plan that ends with warm leads waiting for your reps each morning. Introduction It is 9:12 PM. A purchasing manager needs 500 boxes by Friday. Your store loads slowly. Search returns nothing. The catalog is a PDF. The contact form promises a reply tomorrow. Her next tab answers in seconds. Your site never knew she was there. Nobody complains. Nobody calls. Analytics just shows a short visit. That is a silent exit, and it happens every night. So should you rebuild the store or add an AI chatbot? Short answer: fix whichever of speed, search, product data or price accuracy fails first, then add an answer layer such as ChatSKU so the catalog can reply while your team is offline. Doing both, in that order, is the fastest route. The rest of this guide shows you how to tell where you stand, what a silent exit may be costing you, and what the first 30 days could look like. The store is the foundation. ChatSKU is the answer layer on top. Not sure which comes first for your store? Ask for the free Store + Catalog Review. Virtina looks at your store and your catalog together and sends short written suggestions you can act on. There is no cost and no obligation. What should the first 30 days look like? People also ask Conclusion Frequently asked questions Why do B2B buyers leave a store without asking anyone? B2B buyers leave without asking because asking is harder than opening the next tab. Four small frictions add up to one lost order. 1 Slow pages On a phone the page crawls, so the buyer never reaches the chat or the form. 2 Search finds nothing A part number with a dash in the wrong place returns zero results. 3 Catalog trapped in a PDF Specs and pack sizes sit in a download nobody opens at 9 PM. 4 Reply tomorrow The buyer needs an answer tonight, not a ticket number. Same buyer, same 9 PM. The difference is what sits behind your catalog. Gartner surveyed 632 B2B buyers in 2024 and found that 61% prefer a buying experience without a sales rep. That figure is about buying preference, not chatbots. It still tells you something: buyers want answers on their own, and your store has to give them. What does a silent exit look like in your logs? Look for sessions that end on a search with no results, with no form fill and no call. You never get a complaint, because the buyer never raised a hand. Your sales team hears only from the buyers who stayed. The ones who left look like ordinary traffic. Why does the night matter? Many buyer questions arrive when the buyer’s day is ending. A purchasing manager checks stock after meetings, not during them. If the answer waits until morning, a competitor with a faster path has already replied. What does a silent exit actually cost? You cannot fix what you cannot see, so put a number on it. Use this simple formula with your own data. The formula: after-hours buying questions per month × share that become quote requests × quote-to-order rate × average order value = revenue that quietly left each month. Step Illustrative example Your number After-hours questions with buying intent 40 a month Count them in the inbox, forms and live chat Share that would have become a quote request 1 in 4, so 10 quotes Ask your reps how many ask for a quote Quote-to-order rate 1 in 5, so 2 orders Use your own close rate Average order value $1,500 Use your own average Revenue that left $3,000 a month, $36,000 a year Your result This is an illustration only, not a benchmark and not a client result. Replace every number with your own. Even small inputs show why the question is worth a few minutes this week. If the answer is a number you do not like, the foundation and the answer layer are no longer optional. Can an AI chatbot fix a slow or messy store? No, an AI chatbot cannot fix a slow store or messy product data. It makes answers faster, not correct. Picture a buyer who asks for a fastener sold in packs of 100. If the product record only says “each”, the chat has to guess, and a guess can turn into a wrong quote. A fast wrong answer is worse than a slow form, because the buyer trusts it. It quotes stock that is gone, shows a price that differs from the quote your rep would send, or misses a spec. Empty search has the same root cause. If a part number returns nothing for a human, the chat has nothing to find either. Fixing B2B site search comes before adding any assistant on top. Does speed still matter if the chat is good? Yes, because buyers must reach the chat first. A slow page loses people before they type a word. A 2019 study from Google and Deloitte, titled Milliseconds Make Millions, tracked mobile load times for 30 days and found a 0.1 second speed gain raised conversion by 8.4% on retail sites. That is retail, not B2B, and the study is dated, so B2B behaviour may differ. The direction is still clear, and a slow B2B store diagnostic shows where the seconds go. What should be fixed first, the store or the chat? Fix the store and its product data first, because every later answer is built from them. Fix the foundation first, then let the catalog talk. Virtina has spent more than 14 years and 2,500+ projects building online stores, many for businesses that sell to other businesses. That work covers the platform, page speed, clean product data, search and the links to your ERP and pricing. Your ecommerce website redesign starts from those same layers. Price and stock that match your WooCommerce ERP integration close that gap at the source. What does an AI catalog assistant add after the rebuild? After the store is solid, one gap remains. Buyers ask questions every hour, and your team is not online for all of them. That gap is where ChatSKU sits. What is ChatSKU? ChatSKU is an AI-powered B2B catalog chat and RFQ platform. It reads the product list you already have and turns it into a 24/7 buying assistant that talks to buyers in plain language. It is a separate brand from Virtina, built to sit on top of a clean store. How does it work in three steps? 1 Connect your catalog Start from a PDF, an Excel sheet, an ERP export or a WooCommerce, Magento or BigCommerce store. It goes live with one line of embed code, and setup can take less than a day when the data is clean. 2 Buyers ask in plain language Pack size, specs, fit and availability. It copes with typos, and supports voice and photo search and multiple languages. 3 You get quotes and leads It builds the quote request, captures the order intent and routes it to your team, with customer-group and tiered pricing where you use them. What does a rep see the next morning? This is the part that matters for revenue. Instead of an empty inbox, your team opens a short list of buyers who already asked a question and are ready for a quote. Overnight lead 9:14 PM Buyer: Purchasing manager, mid-size cabinet maker Asked: “Do you have the three-quarter inch fastener in a case of 500?” ChatSKU answered: pack size, stock status and the buyer’s tier price Then: quote request for 500 units, needed by Friday Status: ready for your rep at 8:30 AM Illustrative example, not a client record. The goal: reps start the day with warm leads, not a cold inbox. ChatSKU also shows which questions come up most, so you can fix catalog gaps before they cost another sale. It can connect to your CRM, eCommerce platform or ERP. One honest limit: a fast answer is only as good as the data behind it. That is why the foundation comes first. title: WooCommerce emails not sending? Diagnose it in four steps

text: Summary WooCommerce emails not sending usually means one of four stages failed. The built-in email log names the stage in minutes. You can run the settings, sender and spam checks yourself. A developer takes over when paid orders never reach Processing, the log shows host errors, or you cannot test safely. Handing over the log and your test results shortens the fix. Introduction A silent order inbox is expensive in the weeks before holiday peak. Orders land in the dashboard, yet you and your customers hear nothing. Buyers wonder whether the order went through, and support tickets follow. The usual mistake is installing a mail tool before you know which stage broke. That guesswork costs days and can hide the real cause. This guide walks four stages in order, with a clear point to stop and call a developer. Table of Contents Why do WooCommerce emails go missing, and which stage failed? Was the email ever triggered? Did WooCommerce actually send the email? Did the receiving mailbox accept it? Why do store emails land in spam, and how do you fix it? What is the full checklist to run on one test order? When should you bring in a WooCommerce developer? People also ask Conclusion Frequently asked questions Why do WooCommerce emails go missing, and which stage failed? A missing WooCommerce email fails at one of four stages: never triggered, not sent, not delivered, or landed in spam. Each stage has a different owner and a different first place to look. The table maps all four in the order you should check them. Stage What it means Where to look first 1. Never triggered The order never reached a status that fires the email Order status and the email’s enable switch 2. Not sent WooCommerce tried, and the attempt failed or was skipped WooCommerce, Status, Logs 3. Not delivered The message left your site, but the receiving mailbox refused it From address and mail setup 4. Landed in spam The mailbox accepted the message but filed it as junk SPF, DKIM and DMARC records The four stages of a missing WooCommerce email, in the order to check them. Transactional emails are the messages an order or account action triggers. Examples are order confirmations, status updates, and password resets. They matter more than newsletters because customers act on them. How does an order email travel from checkout to inbox? WooCommerce triggers an email when an order changes status. It hands the message to WordPress through the wp_mail() function. WordPress then passes it to your host’s mail setup. Your host sends it on to the receiving mailbox provider. That provider decides between the inbox and the spam folder. Each handoff is a place where the message can stall. The official guide often points to the host’s mail function when mail fails. Treat that as the usual suspect, not the only one. Silent glitches like this sit on the list of WooCommerce conversion killers . Was the email ever triggered? An email is triggered only when the order reaches a status that fires it, and that email is switched on. Check both before you look at anything else. Most stage-one failures end here. Is the order stuck in Pending payment? Pending payment sends nothing. A customer may have left an external payment page, or a card may have been declined. The exact behavior varies by gateway. If payment succeeded but the status never moved, the gateway failed to report back. That is a payment communication problem, not an email problem. An order that reaches Processing status should fire the notification when it is enabled. Line up the order status, the email entry, and the payment details together. Repeated stalls are a known pattern in WooCommerce checkout failures . They also overlap with wider ecommerce website problems . Is the email switched on and addressed to someone? Open WooCommerce, then Settings, then Emails, and select the template. Tick Enable this email notification and save. Then confirm the recipient field holds a real address. A blank recipient produces a Skipped entry in the log. The next step shows how to read it. Did WooCommerce actually send the email? You can tell in minutes from the transactional-emails log, which marks each attempt sent, failed, disabled, or skipped. Place a test order or trigger the email. Then open WooCommerce, Status, Logs and pick the transactional-emails source. Look for the entry that matches your test. Current WooCommerce versions include this log. The WooCommerce email troubleshooting guide documents each status. What do sent, failed, disabled and skipped mean? Sent. WooCommerce handed the message to the mail system. This is not proof of delivery. Failed. Mail sending returned an error, often with a reason. It usually points to hosting or mail setup. Disabled. That email type is turned off in settings. Skipped. A required condition is missing, such as a recipient. Sent and failed attempts also appear as private notes on the order. Disabled and skipped entries appear only in the log. Recipients show as a username or guest, not a raw address. Illustrative case: paid orders, no new-order email Illustrative example, not a client case. A store owner sees paid orders in the dashboard but never receives the new-order message. The log shows Skipped for each order because the recipient field is blank. After the owner fills in the recipient and places another test order, the log shows Sent. What if the log is empty, or the email is not in it? Open Logs, then Settings, and confirm logging is on. Make sure the threshold is not hiding info or notice entries. No entry at all points to a fatal error or plugin conflict. Test conflicts on a staging site, never on the live store. In practice, switching plugins off on a live checkout risks lost orders. Admin emails and password reset emails may not appear in the WooCommerce log. For those, read the log your SMTP service keeps, or use a mail logging tool. A wider list of common WooCommerce bugs helps when the log shows nothing useful. Did the receiving mailbox accept it? A Sent status only means WooCommerce handed the message onward, so delivery depends on your From address and mail setup. Two settings decide most of what happens next. Deliverability is the final test of both. Does the From address use your own domain? Use an address on your site’s domain in WooCommerce, Settings, Emails. A From address on a free mail domain, such as Gmail, often gets marked as spam or blocked. The sending server does not match the sender the message claims to be. Mailbox providers read that mismatch as a sign of forgery. Your own domain gives them something to verify. The spam section below explains how. Should store mail go through a dedicated SMTP service? The WooCommerce guide recommends a dedicated third-party SMTP service. It is more reliable than your own server’s mail function. An average site usually stays within free tiers. An SMTP service also keeps its own log of what it accepted and refused. That log fills the gap the WooCommerce log leaves for password reset emails. Before you change anything, check the junk folder and the spelling of the recipient address on the test order. A single typo looks exactly like a delivery failure. Rule it out first. Why do store emails land in spam, and how do you fix it? Store emails land in spam when receivers cannot confirm the message really came from your domain. Three DNS records give them that proof. Missing or broken records are the most common fix at this stage. What do SPF, DKIM and DMARC each do? An SPF record lists which servers may send mail for your domain. A DKIM signature marks each message so the receiver can check it against a DNS record. A DMARC policy tells receivers what to do when a message fails both. Domain alignment means the From domain matches the domain that passes those checks. If your host sends your store’s mail, ask the host to confirm all three are set up. If you use an SMTP service, follow its domain authentication steps. What do Gmail’s sender rules require? Since February 2024, the Gmail sender guidelines require SPF or DKIM from every sender. Senders also need valid forward and reverse DNS, plus TLS. Google wants the reported spam rate under 0.3% in Postmaster Tools. Senders of more than 5,000 messages a day to Gmail also need SPF, DKIM and DMARC with aligned domains. Check your own volume to see which tier applies. Yahoo set comparable requirements from the same month. Set up authentication even if you only send transactional emails. Other mailbox providers are likely to follow the same direction. Doing it once protects every order message you send. What is the full checklist to run on one test order? Run seven checks in order on a single test order, and stop at the first one that fails. Fix that item, then place another test order. Do not skip ahead. Step 1. Confirm the order status is Processing, not Pending payment. Step 2. Confirm the email is enabled and has a recipient. Step 3. Read the transactional-emails log entry for the test order. Step 4. If the entry says Sent, check the junk folder and the recipient spelling. Step 5. Confirm the From address uses your own domain. Step 6. Route mail through a dedicated SMTP service and confirm the SPF, DKIM and DMARC records. Step 7. For password reset and admin emails, read the SMTP service’s own log instead. If the same failure returns after a fix, treat it as a developer case. Recurring faults are what ongoing WooCommerce support and maintenance exists to catch. When should you bring in a WooCommerce developer? Bring in a developer when paid orders never reach Processing, the log shows host errors, or you cannot test safely. These cases need server, DNS, or code access that a store owner often lacks. The signs below are specific. Which signs point to a developer-level problem? The decision rule is simple: a WooCommerce bug fix service takes over when any sign below appears. Paid orders whose status never reaches Processing, which points to a gateway callback fault. A Failed log entry with a host-level reason, or no entry plus fatal errors. A suspected plugin or theme conflict and no staging site to test it. No DNS access, or records in place while mail still lands in spam. Custom, B2B approval, or ERP-triggered emails that stopped after an update. The same failure returning after a fix. Updates cause some of these. A change can blank custom fields in emails, as the notes on HPOS plugin compatibility describe. Custom or ERP-triggered messages usually need a WooCommerce development company that can read the integration code. A store takeover service covers stores inherited from another developer, where nobody knows the custom code. What should you hand the developer? Evidence turns an open-ended hunt into a short fix. Send these items with the first message. The log excerpt, with status, reason, and timestamp. Your seven check results, noting where the test failed. Screenshots of the SPF, DKIM, and DMARC DNS records. The From address and mail setup in use, such as your host or an SMTP service. Example order numbers that missed their emails. What changed recently, including updates and new plugins. In practice, a developer will ask for these anyway. Sending them first saves a round of questions. People also ask How do I test WooCommerce emails? Place a test order, then open WooCommerce, Status, Logs and pick the transactional-emails source. The entry shows whether the email was sent, failed, disabled, or skipped. Check the inbox and the junk folder next. Why am I not getting new order emails as the store owner? Check that the new order email is enabled and lists your address as the recipient. Admin emails may not appear in the WooCommerce log. If so, read your SMTP service’s own log. Do emails send when an order is Pending payment? No. Orders in Pending payment do not trigger emails. The order must first reach a status such as Processing. Why do WooCommerce emails go to spam? Receivers often cannot confirm the message came from your domain. A free mail From address or missing authentication records is the usual cause. The spam section above covers the fix. Conclusion A missing order email fails at one of four stages. One log names the stage, so you fix the right thing first. Owner checks come before any developer call. When the evidence points to gateways, host errors, or DNS, hand over the log and your test results. Diagnosing first turns a guess into a short, clear fix. Frequently asked questions What does a Sent status in the WooCommerce email log mean? Sent means WooCommerce handed the message to the mail system. It does not confirm the inbox received it. Check the From address, the spam folder, and mail authentication next. Can a plugin or theme conflict stop store emails? Yes. A conflict can throw an error before the order status changes, so the email never fires. Test on a staging site with other plugins off and a default theme. Do I need a dedicated SMTP service for WooCommerce? The official guide recommends one because it is more reliable than your server’s own mail function. It also gives you a log to read for admin and password reset emails. An average site usually stays within free tiers. Why do password reset emails not show in the WooCommerce log? The WooCommerce log may not record admin and password reset emails. Read your SMTP service’s own log for those. A mail logging tool is the other option. Is it safe to use a free mail address as the From address? No. Free mail domains often cause store messages to be marked as spam or blocked. Use an address on your own domain instead. How do I know whether my host is the problem? Look for Failed entries with a mail sending error in the log. The official guide often points to the host’s mail function in those cases. Ask the host to confirm its mail setup and DNS records, or move store mail to an SMTP service. What should I send a developer to speed up the fix? Send the log excerpt, your test results, and screenshots of your DNS records. Add the From address, mail setup, example order numbers, and recent changes. That package usually saves a round of questions. Virtina helps B2B sellers design, build, and connect online ordering, from pricing rules to ERP hand-offs. The team works across WooCommerce, Magento, BigCommerce, and Shopify.

title: 5 Ecommerce Website Nightmares That Could Scare Away Your Customers
headings: Which ecommerce website problems should you check first?
What should you check before Halloween weekend?
Nightmare 1: Why can’t customers finish checkout?
Nightmare 2: Why do slow pages drive shoppers away?
Nightmare 3: Why does a responsive store still feel bad on a phone?
Nightmare 4: How do you tell a payment failure from a legitimate decline?
Nightmare 5: How do inventory and integration errors create wrong orders?
When to bring in professional help
How do you find out which nightmare is costing you the most?
How can Virtina help you find and fix these problems?
Why do shoppers abandon an online store at checkout?
How can you tell a payment failure from a normal decline?
How often should you test your store checkout?
When is a slow store a sign you need more than quick fixes?
text: HALLOWEEN 2026 · SATURDAY, OCTOBER 31 Is your store ready for the weekend, or will a hidden problem scare your customers away? Summary Halloween lands on a Saturday this year, and any traffic spike is when hidden website problems cost the most. A weak offer is rarely why a store loses sales. Five hidden problems do far more damage. These are a checkout that throws an error, a page that crawls, and a phone layout that fights the shopper. The other two are a payment that fails for no clear reason and an order for stock you lack. Each section shows what the customer sees and how to confirm the cause with tools you already have. It also says when the fix is bigger than a settings change. Introduction The ecommerce website problems that cost the most sales are checkout errors, slow pages, and clumsy mobile buying. Payment failures and stock or integration data that does not match reality complete the list. Each one has a symptom shoppers notice and a fix. You can usually confirm the cause in an hour or two. Halloween is a fair excuse to go looking. This year it falls on a Saturday, so shoppers have a whole weekend to browse and buy. Seasonal promotions send extra traffic to your store. That traffic lands on the same checkout, product pages and payment setup as everyone else’s, right before the holiday rush. The scariest problems are the ones you cannot see. Shoppers rarely report them. They just leave. Most advice on this topic tells you what to improve. This guide is about diagnosis: something is going wrong, so how do you find out what? It works on any platform, with WooCommerce examples where the steps are platform specific. Design and usability problems are a separate topic. Table of Contents Which ecommerce website problems should you check first? What should you check before Halloween weekend? Nightmare 1: Why can’t customers finish checkout? Nightmare 2: Why do slow pages drive shoppers away? Nightmare 3: Why does a responsive store still feel bad on a phone? Nightmare 4: How do you tell a payment failure from a legitimate decline? Nightmare 5: How do inventory and integration errors create wrong orders? How do you find out which nightmare is costing you the most? How can Virtina help you find and fix these problems? People also ask Conclusion Frequently asked questions Which ecommerce website problems should you check first? Start with the problems that stop a sale outright. A broken checkout or a failing payment loses every shopper who hits it. A slow page only loses some of them. This table is the short version of the five sections below. Use it to jump to the one that matches what you are seeing. Problem What the customer sees First check Usual fix Checkout will not complete Button does nothing, no shipping options, valid address rejected Browser console and shipping zones Remove the script conflict or repair the shipping rule Slow pages Blank spaces, images popping in, laggy taps Field data in Search Console and PageSpeed Insights Images, scripts, caching or hosting, depending on the report Mobile frustration Tiny buttons, covered content, stacked pop-ups Buy something on a real phone Larger tap targets, fewer pop-ups, simpler variation pickers Payment failures Payment failed, or charged with no order Order notes, WooCommerce logs and the gateway dashboard Keys, webhooks, firewall rules or a plugin fix Wrong stock and orders Sold out after payment, wrong item, odd shipping cost Compare stock in every system Faster sync, error alerts and clean data mapping What should you check before Halloween weekend? Fifteen minutes now is cheaper than a lost weekend of sales. Run one quick check for each nightmare, on a phone, before the traffic arrives. The same list works before any promotion. Checkout: place a guest test order with an address outside your usual shipping zone. Speed: run your top category page and best-selling product page through PageSpeed Insights and read the real-visitor data first. Mobile: tap through a product page and the cart on a real phone with your cookie banner and pop-ups showing. Payments: scan recent failed orders and your gateway dashboard for clusters of the same error. Stock: compare the ten best sellers, and anything on promotion, against your warehouse or ERP. Fix what you can before the weekend. Leave bigger changes until it is over, and use the sections below when something fails. NIGHTMARE 1 OF 5 · CHECKOUT Nightmare 1: Why can’t customers finish checkout? Usually because something on the page broke, not because the shopper changed their mind. The usual suspects are a script error or a shipping rule that returns no rates. Others are a field that rejects valid input or a cached page showing stale data. What the customer sees The Place order button spins and nothing happens. The page says no shipping options are available. A valid address gets rejected. The total changes between steps. From the shopper’s side the store looks broken. Nobody wants to hand a card to a broken store. Why it matters Checkout is the last step, so every failure here costs a sale from someone who had already decided to buy. These problems also hide well. Your own test orders work because your address sits inside the shipping zone you set up. Your browser also has no conflicting extensions. Likely causes Shipping setup: an address outside every shipping zone or products with no weight or dimensions. Without them a rate calculator cannot quote. Another cause is a carrier plugin that times out. Validation rules: postcode, phone or state fields that reject real formats. Examples are apartment addresses, Canadian postcodes and phone numbers with extensions. Script conflicts: a chat widget, pop-up tool or speed plugin that combines or delays JavaScript. It can stop the checkout button from working, often right after an update. Caching: cart, checkout and account pages served from cache, which shows stale totals. Security rules: a firewall or security plugin that blocks the request that submits the order. How to confirm it Place a test order in a private browser window, as a guest. Use three addresses. Pick one far from your warehouse, one with an apartment number, and one in another country you ship to. Open the browser developer tools (press F12), go to the Console tab and click Place order. Red errors point to a script conflict. Switch to the Network tab and look for a request with a red status such as 403 or 500. A 403 often means a firewall or security rule is blocking it. A 500 means the server hit an error, so check WooCommerce, then Status, then Logs. Compare dates. If checkout completions dropped on a particular day in your analytics, check what changed that day. Common culprits are a plugin update, a theme change or a new script. On a staging copy, switch plugins off in small groups and retest until the clash disappears. Do not do this on the live store. How to fix it Add a catch-all shipping zone and require weights on shippable products. Loosen validation so it accepts real-world formats. Exclude cart and checkout from JavaScript combining, delay settings and page caching. Replace or reconfigure the conflicting plugin, then retest with the same three addresses. If checkout still fails after those checks, consider professional WooCommerce checkout repair . NIGHTMARE 2 OF 5 · SPEED Nightmare 2: Why do slow pages drive shoppers away? Because a page that is slow to show its main image or respond to a tap feels broken. A shopper with other tabs open will not wait to find out. What the customer sees Grey boxes where products should be. Images that appear one at a time. A filter that takes a second to react, and a layout that jumps just as the shopper goes to tap. Why it matters Product and category pages are where shoppers choose what to buy. Google also measures this on real visits, using Core Web Vitals . Google rates the main content as fast when it loads within 2.5 seconds. It says the same for an Interaction to Next Paint of 200 milliseconds or less. Likely causes Large, uncompressed images, especially hero banners and product galleries. Third-party scripts: chat, reviews, heat maps, tracking tags and pop-ups that load on every page. Page caching that is missing or set up wrongly. Slow server response from an under-sized hosting plan. A heavy theme or page builder that ships far more code than the page needs. Plugin database queries, such as filters, related-product widgets and search tools, that run on every category page. How to confirm it Check real-visitor data first. In Google Search Console, open the Core Web Vitals report. In PageSpeed Insights, read the field data at the top before the lab score. Lab scores can swing from one run to the next. Test the pages that make money. Those are a category page, your best-selling product page and the cart, not only the home page. Read what the report blames. A high server response time points to hosting, caching or slow database work. A large image flagged as the Largest Contentful Paint element points to image size or format. A long list of unused JavaScript points to plugins and third-party tags. Open developer tools, go to the Network tab, reload the page and sort by size, then by time. The heaviest file and the slowest request are usually easy to spot. On WordPress, a free plugin such as Query Monitor shows slow database queries and which plugin is running them. How to fix it Match the fix to the finding. Resize and compress the biggest images. Remove tags you no longer use. Turn on page caching, but not for cart and checkout. Ask your host about server response if that was the flagged item. Measure again after each change so you know what worked. Store-specific steps for WooCommerce are covered in WooCommerce speed without switching hosts . If you would rather hand it over, Virtina offers ecommerce performance optimization . NIGHTMARE 3 OF 5 · MOBILE Nightmare 3: Why does a responsive store still feel bad on a phone? Because responsive only means the layout fits the screen. Mobile-friendly means a person can actually buy something with one thumb, on a slow connection, while distracted. What the customer sees Links too close together to tap accurately. A sticky header and cookie bar that cover a third of the screen. Size and colour pickers that need three attempts. A pop-up whose close button sits off screen. A keyboard that hides the field being typed in. Why it matters Plenty of shoppers browse and buy on phones, so a clumsy experience is not a niche problem. It also hides in your numbers. Low mobile conversion gets explained away as shoppers just browsing, when the page itself is often the cause. Likely causes A desktop design squeezed onto a small screen instead of designed for thumbs. Variation selectors, such as dropdowns and tiny swatches, built for a mouse pointer. Stacked overlays: cookie banner, newsletter pop-up, chat bubble and discount bar all at once. Sticky elements that take too much of the viewport. Pages that are too heavy for a mobile network. How to confirm it Complete a purchase on a real mid-range phone on mobile data, and time it. Browser device mode is useful for checking layout, but it cannot reproduce thumb reach or a slow network. In GA4, compare add-to-cart and conversion rates for mobile and desktop. A large gap at one step shows where to look. Watch ten mobile session recordings in a tool such as Microsoft Clarity or Hotjar. Look for repeated taps on things that do not respond. How to fix it Make tap targets roughly 44 to 48 pixels with space between them. Allow one pop-up at most, delayed, with a large close button. Turn variation choices into big buttons instead of small dropdowns. Shrink or remove sticky bars. Wallet buttons and buy now pay later are covered in WooCommerce mobile checkout . NIGHTMARE 4 OF 5 · PAYMENTS Nightmare 4: How do you tell a payment failure from a legitimate decline? Look at the pattern. A legitimate decline belongs to one card or one customer and carries a reason from the bank. A technical failure hits many customers at once. It often shows an error from your own setup instead of a bank reason. It tends to start right after a change. What the customer sees The payment fails with a vague message. A wallet button errors out. A 3-D Secure window opens and never returns. Worst of all, the customer is charged but the order shows as failed or pending. They have to email you to find out what happened. Why it matters A real decline is the bank doing its job, and you cannot fix it. A technical failure is yours to fix, and it keeps costing sales until someone notices. The trouble is that both look like payment failed in your order list. Likely causes Configuration: expired or changed API keys, test mode left on, or a webhook address or secret that no longer matches. Blocked callbacks: a firewall, security plugin or host rule that stops the gateway from reporting back. Paid orders then stay on Pending payment. Authentication steps: 3-D Secure or wallet flows that fail. A script conflict, pop-up blocker or redirect problem stops the shopper returning to your store. Plugin conflicts and outdated payment plugins after a WooCommerce or PHP update. Over-strict fraud rules, in the gateway or in a plugin, that reject genuine customers. How to confirm it Open a failed order and read the order notes. WooCommerce usually records what the gateway returned. Go to WooCommerce, then Status, then Logs, and open the log for your payment gateway. Look for repeated errors with the same message. Open the gateway’s own dashboard and compare. Declines with a bank reason, spread across different customers, are normal. A cluster of API or authentication errors is not. Check timing. Did the failures start after an update, a key change or a plugin install? Look for paid orders stuck on Pending payment. If the gateway shows success and your store does not, the callback is not reaching you. Place a test order using the gateway’s test mode, on a phone and on a desktop. This table gives you a quick way to read what you find. Signal Usually a legitimate decline Usually a technical failure Who is affected One card or one customer Many customers across different cards Message A bank reason, such as insufficient funds or card declined An API, authentication, key or webhook error Timing Scattered across days Starts after a change or an outage Retry Works with another card Fails with every card Order status Failed with a clear reason Pending payment although the gateway shows success Gateway dashboard Decline logged with an issuer reason Errors logged, or no record of the attempt at all How to fix it Re-enter and verify keys in the right mode, and re-register webhooks. Allow the gateway through your firewall rules. Update or replace the conflicting plugin. Loosen fraud rules that block genuine buyers. Keep API keys out of emails and chat messages. If your setup involves several gateways or custom rules, WooCommerce payment gateway integration help is available. NIGHTMARE 5 OF 5 · STOCK AND ORDERS Nightmare 5: How do inventory and integration errors create wrong orders? Because two systems disagree and the website is the one making the promise. When your store, warehouse system, marketplace or ERP hold different numbers, shoppers are sold items you do not have. They can also be charged shipping that does not match reality. What the customer sees An in-stock item followed by a sorry, it sold out email. The wrong variant arriving. A shipping cost that looks off, a delivery date that slips, or no tracking number after the order. Why it matters These failures happen after payment, so they cost more than a lost sale. The costs include refunds, support time, a customer who does not come back and sometimes a public review. Likely causes Slow sync: stock updated nightly or every few hours, so fast sellers oversell in between. Silent failures: a sync job fails, nobody is alerted, and the numbers drift for weeks. Several channels selling the same stock with nothing reserved when an order arrives. Mismatched SKUs or variation mapping between systems. Orders that never reach the warehouse or ERP because a field is missing or an API limit is hit. Out-of-date shipping data, such as missing weights or old rate tables. How to confirm it Pick ten best-selling products and compare stock in every system on the same day. Check the website, the warehouse or ERP, and any marketplace. Find the last successful sync and read its log. If your integration uses scheduled tasks, WooCommerce, then Status, then Scheduled Actions shows failed or overdue jobs. Take your last five oversold or wrong orders and trace each one. Note when it was placed, what stock the site showed, and what the other system said at that moment. Send a test order all the way through to the warehouse or ERP. Check the label, tracking number and customer email. Read support emails for phrases like out of stock after I paid or wrong item. They show patterns your reports miss. How to fix it Move fast-selling items from scheduled sync to near real-time sync. Pick one system as the source of truth. Keep a small safety buffer on scarce items. Set alerts for failed sync jobs and reconcile counts weekly. Clean up SKU mapping before you change anything else. When to bring in professional help Get help when three or more systems are involved. Custom integrations and middleware call for help too. So do logs that show errors you cannot interpret. Help is also worth getting when a fix would change how orders flow to the warehouse. ERP, warehouse and marketplace connections fall under ecommerce integration services . WooCommerce stores that mainly need accurate counts across channels can look at WooCommerce stock management plugin options . How do you find out which nightmare is costing you the most? Every horror story has a moment when someone finally turns the lights on. This is that moment for your store. Follow the money in order. Check where shoppers drop off, then check the technical reports for that step. Thirty minutes is enough to point you at the right nightmare. Open your funnel in GA4 and note the biggest drop between product view, cart, checkout and purchase, split by device. If the drop happens before checkout, run the speed and mobile checks from Nightmares 2 and 3. If the drop happens at checkout, test with three addresses and read the console, as in Nightmare 1. If shoppers reach payment and fail, review failed orders and gateway logs, as in Nightmare 4. If sales complete but customers complain afterwards, audit stock and sync, as in Nightmare 5. Repeat this monthly and after any plugin, theme or gateway change, since most of these problems start with a change. If the same problems keep returning, the platform or theme may be the cause. Weigh that with ecommerce website redesign warning signs , which help you judge whether to keep patching. Heading into the holiday rush? Run this triage first. Then work through the WooCommerce holiday season checklist . How can Virtina help you find and fix these problems? Virtina has built and supported ecommerce stores for more than 14 years. The team starts with an audit rather than a rebuild. Checkout, speed, mobile experience, payments and integrations are checked in the order described above. Each finding is marked as a quick fix or a structural issue. A second pair of eyes is available through ecommerce support . Tell Virtina which symptom you are seeing, and it will say what to check first. Virtina runs the checks above. It sends back a short, prioritized list of what is real and what is not. People also ask Why do shoppers abandon an online store at checkout? Shoppers leave when checkout breaks, slows down, or surprises them. A script error, a missing shipping rate, or a rejected field can stop a sale outright. Most shoppers never report it. They simply leave. How can you tell a payment failure from a normal decline? A technical failure hits many customers at once and often shows an error from your own setup. It tends to start right after a change. A normal decline is a single bank reason on a single order. How often should you test your store checkout? Test it monthly and after any plugin, theme or gateway change. Use a guest order on a real phone. Check the order, the email and the payment record each time. When is a slow store a sign you need more than quick fixes? Quick fixes work when a few heavy images or old tags cause the delay. If the same problems keep returning, the platform or theme may be the cause. That is the point to weigh a redesign instead of more patching. Conclusion Most of these nightmares are not mysteries. Each one leaves clues in places you can already reach. Examples are a browser console, an order note, a gateway dashboard and a stock comparison. Look at the step where shoppers drop off. Confirm the cause before you change anything. Fix one thing at a time so you can tell what worked. The best time to find a broken checkout is before a customer does. Place one test order today, on a phone, as a guest. Halloween ends on October 31, but a broken checkout will still be there on November 1 unless someone fixes it. Frequently Asked Questions How often should I test my checkout? Place one real test order at least weekly, and again after every plugin, theme, gateway or hosting change. Use a different device and address each time so you do not keep testing the same path. Is it safe to troubleshoot on my live store? Reading logs, order notes and reports is safe. Turning plugins off, changing settings or testing code is not, because shoppers are using the store while you do it. Use a staging copy for anything that changes behaviour, and take a full backup first. What should I send a developer when I report a checkout or payment bug? Send the page address, the device and browser, and the time it happened. Add the order number if there is one and the exact message shown. Include a screenshot of the browser console if you can capture it. Steps to repeat the problem matter most. Never include API keys or passwords in the message. How can I find out about these problems before customers tell me? Set up uptime monitoring and an alert for failed orders and stalled payments. Add a daily look at the gateway dashboard and a conversion-drop alert in your analytics. Keep a recurring test order on your calendar too. Do these problems affect SEO as well as sales? Slow pages can, since page experience is one of many signals Google considers. Checkout, payment and stock problems do not affect rankings directly, but they waste the traffic you worked to earn. Are hosted platforms like Shopify free of these problems? They remove some, such as server setup and plugin conflicts on the core store, but not all. Payment configuration, third-party apps, mobile design and integrations with your warehouse or ERP can still cause every nightmare here.

title: WooCommerce vs BigCommerce for Growing Stores: Which Is Better in 2026?
headings: Which is better for a growing store, WooCommerce or BigCommerce?
How do WooCommerce and BigCommerce compare side by side?
How much does each platform really cost?
Does BigCommerce charge transaction fees, and does WooCommerce?
Which platform is easier to run day to day?
Which one handles growth and B2B better?
How do they compare for SEO and speed?
When should you choose WooCommerce, and when BigCommerce?
Can you switch from one to the other later?
text: Summary For most growing stores, WooCommerce is the better fit if you want full control, custom features and costs that do not step up with revenue. BigCommerce is the better fit if you want a hosted platform with strong built-in features and less technical upkeep. WooCommerce costs less at the platform level but needs hosting, security and maintenance. BigCommerce costs more as your sales grow but looks after hosting and updates for you. This guide compares cost, fees, features, B2B and growth, then gives a simple way to decide. Prices are as published in October 2026 and can change. Introduction When a store outgrows its starter setup, the platform question gets real fast. WooCommerce and BigCommerce both power serious stores, but they work in opposite ways. One is software you own and host. The other is a hosted service you rent. That difference shapes almost everything else: what you pay as you grow, how far you can customize, who looks after security, and how hard it is to leave later. Virtina builds on both platforms, so this comparison is meant to help you choose, not to push one answer. If you are also weighing Shopify or Magento, our four-platform comparison guide covers all four. Table of Contents Which is better for a growing store, WooCommerce or BigCommerce? How do WooCommerce and BigCommerce compare side by side? How much does each platform really cost? Does BigCommerce charge transaction fees, and does WooCommerce? Which platform is easier to run day to day? Which one handles growth and B2B better? How do they compare for SEO and speed? When should you choose WooCommerce, and when BigCommerce? Can you switch from one to the other later? Which is better for a growing store, WooCommerce or BigCommerce? Neither platform wins for every store. Choose WooCommerce when you need deep customization, want to pick your own hosting, sell through WordPress content, or want costs that do not rise with revenue. Choose BigCommerce when you want a hosted store with strong built-in features and predictable upkeep, and your team would rather not manage servers, updates and security patches. A simple rule works well here. If your edge is a custom buying experience, lean WooCommerce. If your edge is operations and you want the platform to just run, lean BigCommerce. How do WooCommerce and BigCommerce compare side by side? This table shows the differences that matter most when a store is growing. Factor WooCommerce BigCommerce Platform cost Free plugin on WordPress Monthly subscription (Core, Growth, Scale or Performance) Hosting You choose and pay for it, from shared to managed plans Included in the plan Sales limits None Plans are tied to sales. Core and Growth upgrade automatically, and Scale adds 0.9% above its monthly cap Payment fees Only the gateway’s own fees No platform fee on listed providers. Extra fee on other providers, plus the gateway’s own fees Design Any WordPress theme or a fully custom build BigCommerce themes, custom themes or a headless build Built-in features Added through extensions Many included, such as multi-currency, coupons, reviews and a blog Customization Open code, almost no limits Strong through APIs and themes, within platform rules B2B tools Extensions or custom build Customer groups from Growth, price lists on Performance Upkeep and security Your team or an agency Platform manages hosting and core updates Data ownership You hold the files and database Data lives on the platform while you subscribe, with export options Treat the table as a starting point. Your catalog, checkout rules and integrations decide which column matters most. How much does each platform really cost? WooCommerce looks cheaper on paper because the plugin is free, but the real cost is spread across hosting, extensions, development and care. Market estimates put hosting from about $25 a month for shared plans to around $200 a month for high-performance setups, premium extensions at roughly $500 to $2,000 a year, and maintenance at $1,000 to $5,000 a year. For a full breakdown, read our guide on how much a WooCommerce website costs . BigCommerce publishes its prices. Core is $39 a month ($29 billed annually), Growth is $105 ($79 annually), Scale is $399 ($299 annually), and Performance starts at $1,499 a month billed annually. Hosting is included, but plans follow your sales, so the bill steps up as you grow. Prices are in USD, exclude tax, and were read from BigCommerce’s pricing page in October 2026. On both platforms, budget for these extras: WooCommerce: premium extensions, backups, security monitoring and developer time. BigCommerce: plan upgrades as sales grow, paid apps, premium themes and developer time. Does BigCommerce charge transaction fees, and does WooCommerce? BigCommerce charges no platform fee on orders paid through its listed providers, such as BigCommerce Payments, Stripe, PayPal Braintree and Adyen. Orders paid through other providers add a monthly fee on the sales they process: 2.0% on Core, 1.0% on Growth and 0.6% on Scale. That sits on top of the gateway’s own fees. WooCommerce adds no platform fee. You pay the gateway’s fees, plus any charge from a paid payment extension. If you already rely on a regional or niche payment provider, check this point first, because it can change the math. Which platform is easier to run day to day? BigCommerce is easier for teams without technical staff. Hosting, updates and core security are handled for you, so there is less to monitor. WooCommerce is simple for daily tasks such as editing products and processing orders, especially if your team already uses WordPress. The extra work is behind the scenes: keeping WordPress, plugins and PHP updated, running backups and watching for security issues. A managed host or an agency care plan removes most of that load. Which one handles growth and B2B better? Both platforms scale, in different ways. BigCommerce scales by moving you up plans, with tools such as customer groups from the Growth plan and price lists on Performance. WooCommerce scales by improving hosting and architecture, and its B2B features come from extensions or custom work, such as wholesale pricing, quote requests and ERP connections. Stores with unusual pricing rules or integrations usually find WooCommerce easier to shape. Stores that want these tools ready to use often prefer BigCommerce. For an example of weighing both against a regulated catalog, see how we approached the platform choice for a healthcare store . How do they compare for SEO and speed? Both can rank well. WooCommerce gives you full control over URLs, schema and content through WordPress, which helps content-led stores. BigCommerce includes solid SEO basics and a built-in blog, with less control over server-level changes. Speed depends on setup. WooCommerce needs good hosting, caching and clean extensions. BigCommerce provides a managed environment, so speed depends more on your theme and apps. When should you choose WooCommerce, and when BigCommerce? Choose WooCommerce if: You need custom checkout, pricing or product features. You want to control hosting, data and costs as revenue grows. Content and SEO on WordPress are a big part of your growth. Choose BigCommerce if: You want a hosted store with strong built-in features. Your team prefers not to manage servers, updates and security. You are comfortable with plan prices that follow your sales. If WooCommerce fits, our WooCommerce development services cover builds, migrations and ongoing care. Can you switch from one to the other later? Yes. Products, customers and orders can move in either direction, but URLs, redirects, order history, reviews and integrations need planning to protect rankings and revenue. Pick a quiet sales period, and test checkout, tax and shipping before launch. If BigCommerce looks like the better home, see our BigCommerce development services for build and migration support. Conclusion WooCommerce gives growing stores control and flexibility, while BigCommerce gives them a managed platform with strong built-in tools. The right choice depends on how custom your store is and how much upkeep your team wants to carry. If you want a clear recommendation for your store, contact Virtina and share your catalog, integrations and goals. We can review both options against your needs. Frequently Asked Questions Is BigCommerce good for small stores? It can be, especially if you want hosting and security handled for you. Small stores should compare the Core plan, its sales limit and any payment provider fee with the all-in cost of WooCommerce hosting and care. Do I need a developer for either platform? Not to launch a simple store on either one. Most growing stores still use a developer for design changes, integrations and performance work, more often on WooCommerce because it is open and flexible. Who owns my store data on each platform? With WooCommerce you hold the database and files. With BigCommerce you can export your data, but it lives on the platform while you subscribe. Check the export options before you commit. Can I sell on marketplaces and social channels with both? Yes. Both connect to major marketplaces and social channels, through built-in channel tools on BigCommerce and extensions on WooCommerce. Which is better for a store with thousands of products? Both handle large catalogs. WooCommerce needs strong hosting and database tuning at that size, while BigCommerce manages it for you within its plan and API limits.

title: Holiday Returns Without the Headache: A Simple Returns Policy Guide for Online Stores
headings: Why do holiday returns hurt more than regular returns?
What should a WooCommerce returns policy include?
How long should your holiday return window be?
How do you process a refund in WooCommerce?
How do you handle return requests without a messy inbox?
Should you charge for return shipping?
How can you cut avoidable returns before they happen?
How do you turn a return into a second sale?
What returns mistakes should you avoid?
What does a simple returns checklist look like?
How does Virtina help with WooCommerce returns?
text: Summary Returns peak right after the holidays, and the stores that handle them well keep both the customer and the profit. A clear returns policy also helps you sell before the sale, because shoppers read it before they buy. This guide covers what to put in a WooCommerce returns policy, how to set up refunds and return requests, and how to cut avoidable returns before they happen. Introduction A returns policy is not only a legal page. It is a sales page. Many shoppers read it before they add anything to the cart, and an unclear one sends them to a competitor. The short answer: write the policy in plain words, set up WooCommerce so your staff can act in minutes, and fix the product page problems that cause most returns. This article stays on returns. For checkout and payment options, see our holiday readiness checklist . Table of Contents Why do holiday returns hurt more than regular returns? What should a WooCommerce returns policy include? How long should your holiday return window be? How do you process a refund in WooCommerce? How do you handle return requests without a messy inbox? Should you charge for return shipping? How can you cut avoidable returns before they happen? How do you turn a return into a second sale? What returns mistakes should you avoid? What does a simple returns checklist look like? How does Virtina help with WooCommerce returns? Frequently Asked Questions Why do holiday returns hurt more than regular returns? Gifts come back more often than items people buy for themselves. The buyer is not the user, so size, color and taste are guesses. Orders also arrive in a rush, your team is busy, and the returns land in January when sales slow down. The National Retail Federation has reported that returns cost US retailers hundreds of billions of dollars a year, and online orders tend to come back more often than store purchases. Your own rate depends on your products, so pull last January’s numbers before you plan. The refund is only part of the cost. You also pay for return shipping, handling, repackaging, and items you cannot resell. A good process keeps all of these small. What should a WooCommerce returns policy include? Keep it short enough to read in one minute. Use a plain heading for each of these parts: Part What to say Return window The number of days, and when the clock starts (delivery date or ship date) Eligible items Unused, original packaging, tags attached, plus exceptions such as final sale, custom or perishable goods How to start a return One clear step: a form, an email address, or a link in the order account Refund method Original payment method, store credit, or exchange, and how long it takes Return shipping Who pays, and how to get a label Damaged or wrong items A separate, faster path with photo proof Avoid legal jargon. If you sell in several countries or regulated categories, have a lawyer review the final wording. This guide is general information, not legal advice. In WooCommerce, create the policy as a normal page, then link it in the footer, on product pages, and in order confirmation emails. A policy nobody can find does not build trust. How long should your holiday return window be? Many stores extend the window for gifts, for example by accepting returns until late January on orders placed in November and December. This removes the fear of buying early and can lift conversion. Pick a window you can afford. A longer window means more returns arrive late, when seasonal items have lost value. A practical middle path is a fixed end date stated in the policy and on the cart page, rather than a rolling count of days that confuses shoppers. Write the date in full. “Returns accepted until January 31” is clearer than “30 days from purchase” when someone is buying a gift in October. How do you process a refund in WooCommerce? WooCommerce has refunds built in. Open the order, click Refund, enter the items and amounts, and choose how to refund. Refund via the payment gateway: the money goes back to the customer’s card automatically, if your gateway supports it. This suits most standard returns. Manual refund: WooCommerce records the refund, but you send the money yourself. This suits bank transfers, cash on delivery, or gateways without refund support. Also decide how stock is handled. You can restock returned items from the same refund screen, but only after the item is inspected and back on the shelf. Restocking too early leads to overselling. Test a refund on a small order before the season starts. Check that the customer receives the refund email and that your accounting tool shows the change. Taxes and partial refunds are the usual surprises. How do you handle return requests without a messy inbox? WooCommerce does not include a full return request workflow in its core. Many stores start with a simple contact form that asks for the order number, item, reason, and photos. This works for small volumes. When requests grow, a returns or warranty request plugin can give customers a form in their account, track each request’s status, and email both sides at every step. Check that any plugin you pick works with your WooCommerce version and theme, and test it on a staging copy first. Whichever route you choose, set three rules. Reply within one business day. Give every request a status: received, approved, shipped, or refunded. Keep a template email for each status so staff do not write from scratch during peak weeks. Should you charge for return shipping? There is no single right answer. It depends on your margin and your product. Approach Upside Downside Free returns Builds trust, helps first-time buyers Encourages ordering several sizes, higher cost Flat fee deducted from the refund Covers part of the cost, discourages casual returns Some shoppers see it as a barrier Free only for exchanges or defects Rewards keeping the sale, fair on errors Needs clear rules A common middle option is free return shipping when the problem is your fault (wrong or damaged item) and a small flat fee for change of mind. State it clearly so nobody is surprised. How can you cut avoidable returns before they happen? Most avoidable returns come from a gap between what the shopper expected and what arrived. Closing that gap costs less than processing the return. Start with your return reasons. Export last season’s refunds and sort them: size, color, “not as described”, damaged, late. The top two reasons show you where to work. Then fix the product pages: Return reason Fix on the product page Wrong size or fit Add a size chart, model height, and a “runs small or large” note from real customer feedback Color looks different Use photos in natural light and show the item next to a familiar object Not as described Add dimensions, materials, and what is included in the box Damaged in transit Improve the packaging and mention it on the page Arrived too late for the gift Show clear order-by dates for delivery before the holiday Customer reviews with photos also help, because real pictures set honest expectations. Our guide to common eCommerce UX problems covers more product page issues that lead to disappointed buyers. How do you turn a return into a second sale? A returned item does not have to mean a lost customer. Offer an exchange first on the return form, because swapping a size keeps the revenue. Offer store credit second, perhaps with a small bonus if your margin allows. After the refund, send a short, friendly email. Thank the customer, confirm the refund date, and suggest two or three similar products. Keep it helpful rather than pushy. Track who returns often. A small group usually causes most of the cost, and you can apply stricter terms to them without changing the experience for everyone else. What returns mistakes should you avoid? Hiding the policy in the footer only. Shoppers want to see it near the Add to Cart button. Changing the policy mid-season. Orders follow the terms shown at purchase, so announce changes ahead of time and keep a dated copy. Promising refund times you cannot meet. Say “within 5 to 10 business days of receiving the item” only if your team can do it. Skipping return checks. Returns abuse exists, from empty boxes to swapped items. Inspect returns, keep photos, and use order notes to record what arrived. Ignoring chargebacks. A fast, friendly refund is usually cheaper than a payment dispute, which costs a fee and your time. What does a simple returns checklist look like? Use this simple timeline so nothing is left for the busy weeks. Now: review last season’s refund reasons, write or update the policy page, and test one full refund. Two weeks before Black Friday: add size charts and better photos to your top sellers, and set up your status email templates. Launch week: link the policy on product pages and in order emails, and brief your support staff. December: show the extended gift return date and watch the volume of requests. January: process returns daily, restock only inspected items, and note what to change next year. If you are also planning traffic and promotions, our Black Friday preparation guide covers the selling side. How does Virtina help with WooCommerce returns? We build and support WooCommerce stores for businesses across the US. Our team can set up return request forms, connect refund workflows to your payment gateway, and tidy the order emails your customers receive. Want a second pair of eyes on your store before the season? Talk to our WooCommerce team or keep things running smoothly with WooCommerce support . Conclusion Write a plain policy, set up refunds so any team member can process one, and fix the product page gaps that cause the most returns. Do this before the sale starts, not during it. Start with last year’s refund reasons today, finish your policy a week before Black Friday, and avoid changing terms mid-season. Frequently Asked Questions Is a returns policy required for a WooCommerce store? Rules vary by country, state and product type. Even where it is not required, a clear policy reduces disputes and builds trust. Ask a qualified professional if you sell regulated goods or sell abroad. Can I offer store credit instead of a refund? Often yes, if you state it in your policy before purchase, but local consumer rules may still give buyers a right to a refund in some cases. Check the rules where you sell. Does WooCommerce restock returned items automatically? Not by default. You choose to restock from the refund screen, so do it after you have inspected the item. What if a customer returns an item after the window? You can decide case by case. Many owners make exceptions for loyal customers and for gifts, and note the reason on the order so staff stay consistent. How do I stop customers from ordering many sizes and returning most? Improve size guidance, show real fit feedback, and consider a small fee on change-of-mind returns while keeping defects free. Should I accept returns on sale items? That is your choice. title: What Does a Magento 2 Migration Checklist and Cost Look Like?

text: Summary Migrating to Magento 2 (Adobe Commerce) takes planning in six areas: data, extensions, theme, integrations, SEO and testing. Cost depends mainly on catalog size, custom code and the number of extensions that need rebuilding. A typical project runs from several weeks to a few months, and a staged migration with a final data sync keeps downtime to a few hours or less. Introduction Magento 1 reached end of life years ago, and many stores still run old versions with security and speed problems. Moving to Magento 2 fixes both, but it is not a simple upgrade. It is a rebuild of your theme, extensions and data on a new codebase. This guide gives you a checklist, the factors that drive cost, and the risks to plan for. For help, see our Magento migration services . Table of Contents What does a Magento 2 migration involve? What is the Magento 2 migration checklist? What affects the cost of a Magento migration? How long does a Magento 2 migration take? How do you keep your SEO during the migration? Is Magento 2 the right choice, or should you consider other platforms? What mistakes make Magento migrations go wrong? Which Magento versions need to be migrated? How does the Magento Data Migration Tool work? What happens to your extensions and custom code? How should you handle the theme and site speed? How do you keep downtime close to zero? What should you monitor after the Magento 2 launch? How should you plan the budget for a Magento 2 migration? What hosting does Magento 2 need? How does migration improve security and compliance? What does a typical Magento 1 to Magento 2 project look like? What questions should you ask a Magento migration partner? Who do you need on the project? What does a Magento 2 migration involve? A migration moves your products, customers, orders and settings into a fresh Magento 2 install. Your theme and custom extensions cannot be copied across, so they are rebuilt or replaced. The official Data Migration Tool handles most database content. Everything else is manual work. What is the Magento 2 migration checklist? Audit the current store: products, extensions, custom code and integrations. Decide which extensions to keep, replace or drop. Set up Magento 2 on staging with hosting that meets its requirements. Migrate data using the Data Migration Tool, then clean up errors. Rebuild or choose a new theme and test on mobile. Reconnect payments, shipping, ERP and marketing tools. Map old URLs to new ones with 301 redirects. Run full tests, then a final data sync and go live. What affects the cost of a Magento migration? Cost is driven by scope rather than by the platform license. Factor Lower cost Higher cost Catalog size Under 1,000 products Tens of thousands of SKUs Design Ready made theme Custom design Extensions Few, all compatible Many or custom built Integrations Standard payments and shipping ERP, CRM, custom APIs Hosting Shared or managed basic Cloud with scaling Ask for a written scope so testing, redirects and data cleanup are included in the quote. How long does a Magento 2 migration take? Simple stores can finish in six to ten weeks. Complex stores with many integrations often need three to six months. The longest steps are usually extension replacement and testing, so start those early. How do you keep your SEO during the migration? Keep URL structures the same where you can, redirect every changed URL and carry over titles, descriptions and structured data. Submit the new sitemap on launch day and watch Search Console for crawl errors. Is Magento 2 the right choice, or should you consider other platforms? Magento 2 suits complex catalogs, B2B pricing and heavy customization. If your needs are simpler, Shopify or WooCommerce can cost less to run. Read our Magento to Shopify migration guide to compare. What mistakes make Magento migrations go wrong? Underestimating extension compatibility. No staging environment. Skipping the redirect map. Going live without a final data sync. Ignoring site speed and caching setup. Which Magento versions need to be migrated? Magento 1 stores must move, because that version no longer gets security patches. Many stores on early Magento 2 releases are also behind and should be upgraded to a current supported version. If you are not sure what you run, check the admin footer or ask your developer. The answer decides whether you need a full migration or an upgrade. Our Magento upgrade services cover the second case. How does the Magento Data Migration Tool work? The official Data Migration Tool copies your database content, such as products, customers, orders and settings, into the new Magento 2 database. It runs in stages: settings first, then data, then a final delta sync for new orders. The tool does not move your theme, your custom code or your extensions. Those are separate tasks, which is why a migration is closer to a rebuild than a simple copy. Run it several times on a test copy before launch. Each run shows data errors you can fix, so the final run on launch day is clean and fast. What happens to your extensions and custom code? Extensions built for Magento 1 do not work on Magento 2. For each one, you have three choices: replace it with a Magento 2 version, replace it with a different extension, or rebuild the feature as custom code. List every extension and ask whether you still need it. Many stores find that a third of them are unused, and dropping those saves cost, speeds up the store and reduces security risk. Keep: the extension has a Magento 2 version that fits. Replace: a better or more modern option exists. Rebuild: the feature is unique to your business. Drop: nobody uses it any more. How should you handle the theme and site speed? A migration is a good moment to fix speed. Modern themes and a clean extension list can cut load times a lot compared with an old Magento 1 store. Plan for full page caching, image compression and a content delivery network. Test on a phone, since most shoppers browse on mobile. If you are considering a modern front end, see our work on Magento Hyva theme development . How do you keep downtime close to zero? The safest method is to build the new store beside the old one and keep both running. Customers keep ordering on the old store while the new one is tested. On launch day, freeze the old store briefly, run the final delta sync for new orders, switch the domain and test a live order. With good preparation, this takes a few hours. What should you monitor after the Magento 2 launch? The first weeks after launch show whether the plan worked. Watch error logs, checkout success rate, page speed and Search Console crawl reports. Fix redirect gaps quickly, because each missing redirect is a lost visitor and a lost ranking signal. Keep a short list of issues and review it every few days. If you want a partner for the process, see our Magento migration services . How should you plan the budget for a Magento 2 migration? Split the budget into five parts: discovery and planning, data migration, theme and design, extensions and integrations, and testing with launch support. Seeing them separately makes quotes easier to compare. Keep a contingency of about fifteen to twenty percent. Unknown extension issues and data surprises are normal in Magento projects, and a reserve keeps them from stopping the launch. Ask each provider what is included in testing and in the weeks after launch. Cheap quotes often leave these out, then charge for them later. What hosting does Magento 2 need? Magento 2 is heavier than many platforms, so hosting matters a great deal. It needs a modern PHP version, Elasticsearch or OpenSearch, a database with enough memory and a caching layer such as Varnish or Redis. Shared hosting rarely works. Choose managed Magento hosting or a cloud setup that can scale for traffic spikes, and test it with real catalog data before launch. Slow hosting is one of the most common reasons a new Magento 2 store disappoints. How does migration improve security and compliance? Magento 1 no longer receives patches, which puts card data and customer records at risk and can cause problems with payment compliance. Moving to a supported version restores regular security updates. Use the migration to tidy permissions, remove old admin accounts and enable two factor authentication. Our Magento security tips guide covers the settings worth checking after launch. What does a typical Magento 1 to Magento 2 project look like? Imagine a store with 5,000 products, twenty extensions and a custom checkout. The first step is an audit, which reveals that six extensions are unused and four have no Magento 2 equivalent. The team keeps ten extensions, replaces four, rebuilds one feature as custom code and drops the rest. They migrate data into a test copy, run the tool three times and fix errors each round. A new lightweight theme replaces the old one, and page speed improves clearly. Launch day involves a final sync of new orders, a domain switch and a live test order. The old store stays available for a month as a safety net. What questions should you ask a Magento migration partner? A good partner answers specifics, not slogans. Ask these before you sign. How will you handle my extensions, one by one? What is included in testing and post launch support? How will you protect my SEO and redirect old URLs? Who owns the code and the hosting accounts at the end? Can I see examples of similar migrations? Who do you need on the project? A migration needs a project manager, a Magento developer, a front end developer, a QA tester and someone from your side who knows the business. Small projects combine roles, but each task still needs an owner. Name one person on your team to approve decisions quickly. Slow approvals are a hidden cause of delay and extra cost. Conclusion A good Magento 2 migration is planned, staged and tested. Know your scope, budget for extensions and redirects, and keep the old store running until the new one is stable. Need an expert team? Explore our Magento development services or request a quote for Magento migration . Frequently Asked Questions Do I have to migrate from Magento 1 to Magento 2? Magento 1 no longer receives security updates, so staying on it is a risk. Moving to Magento 2 or another platform is strongly recommended. Can I keep my Magento 1 theme? No. Themes and custom extensions must be rebuilt or replaced for Magento 2. How much downtime should I expect? With a staged migration and a final data sync, downtime is usually a few hours or less. Will my orders and customers be moved? Yes. The Data Migration Tool moves products, customers and orders, though passwords may need resetting. How long does the migration take? Simple stores take about six to ten weeks. Complex stores can take three to six months. What is the biggest cost driver? Custom code and extension replacement are usually the largest costs, followed by design and integrations.
