It means the listing does not say, so ask the publisher or test on staging before you commit. How does each option connect to your checkout? Authorize.Net. This is the best documented option. The official extension supports Accept.js, which keeps card entry off your server, and saved cards through Authorize.Net CIM. It works with merchant accounts in the United States, Canada, Australia and New Zealand. The listing makes no high-risk claims, so approval still depends on the acquirer behind your account. Soar Payments and Payment Nerds both describe Authorize.Net as a gateway used through a high-risk acquirer. NMI. NMI is a gateway layer that many high-risk acquirers resell. The WooCommerce plugins we found are published by third parties, not by NMI itself. The Gain Commerce plugin tokenizes cards in the browser with NMI Collect.js, supports Apple Pay and Google Pay, and adds bot protection with reCAPTCHA v3 or Cloudflare Turnstile. AGMS Pay also uses Collect.js and adds 3D Secure, but its listing says subscriptions are not available yet. USAePay. The plugin on WordPress.org is published by an independent developer, not by USAePay, and takes payments without redirecting the customer. The free version covers refunds from the dashboard and authorize-only transactions. Subscriptions, pre-orders, ACH and saved cards need the paid Advanced version. CCBill. CCBill publishes its own plugin and handles payment entry on its side, so no card data is stored on your WooCommerce site. It offers two integration methods, Advanced Integration and FlexForms. CCBill lists industries such as adult, dating and CBD on its own site, so it is worth a look if mainstream gateways have refused you. Which merchant account providers pair with these gateways? Providers such as PaymentCloud, Soar Payments and Bankful appear most often in 2026 high-risk WooCommerce guides. They are merchant account providers, not WooCommerce plugins. Soar Payments says it supports Authorize.Net, NMI and USAePay, and states that many applications are approved within 48 to 72 hours. That is a vendor claim, not a guarantee, and approval depends on your documents and chargeback history. For the full list of 15 processors with fees, reserve types and chargeback costs, use our high-risk payment processing guide . We keep that comparison in one place on purpose, so this page does not compete with it. What should you check on a gateway plugin before installing it? A gateway can be approved by your processor and still fail at checkout if the plugin is out of date. Our WooCommerce payment gateway integration team sees this often in 2026, mostly with older plugins. Check these five things on the listing before you install: Block checkout support. Newer WooCommerce stores use the block-based checkout, and a plugin that does not register for it can leave the payment method missing. HPOS compatibility. A plugin that reads the old posts table can lose orders. See our guide to migrating to HPOS . Free versus paid features. Subscriptions are paid-only on the USAePay and Gain Commerce plugins. Who publishes it. Official plugin or independent developer? Independent plugins can still be good, but you own the support risk. Recent updates. Look at the last update date and the WordPress and WooCommerce versions it was tested with. Can you trust the high risk gateway plugins on WordPress.org? Treat them with caution. The WordPress.org tag for high-risk payment gateways lists only three plugins today. Their active installs are 40+, 10+ and fewer than 10, and two of them accept crypto. Some advertise instant approval. Small install counts are not proof of a problem, but they mean few stores have tested the plugin under real chargeback and refund pressure. Before using any of them, confirm who the real payment processor is, whether card data is tokenized before it reaches your server, and what happens to your funds if the provider closes your account. Which setup fits which kind of store? Match the plugin features to the way you actually sell, then confirm the processor accepts your category. Store type What to look for Subscription or membership store A plugin with recurring billing support. Authorize.Net, CCBill, and the paid add-ons for NMI and USAePay list it. Avoid unclear free-trial pricing, which Stripe lists as prohibited. CBD or hemp WooPayments sends CBD to Square or Viva Wallet, but see our Square account closure guide before relying on that route. Vape and tobacco Prohibited on WooPayments. Plan around a high-risk merchant account first, then choose the gateway it supports. Adult or dating Look at specialists such as CCBill, which lists these industries and publishes its own WooCommerce plugin. Supplements WooPayments bars products with unsubstantiated claims. Keep your product claims clean and your chargeback ratio low before you apply. What does it take to connect a high risk gateway to WooCommerce? Once the merchant account is approved, the technical work is smaller than the approval, but it is where launches slip. The usual path is: review the gateway, build in a sandbox, add the checkout, set risk controls such as 3D Secure, test the order flow, then go live. We run eight transaction states on staging before launch, including declines, refunds and partial captures. If you want a second pair of eyes before you commit to a plugin, our team can review your gateway choice for block checkout and HPOS fit. Start with our WooCommerce payment gateway integration page. How should you pick in the next week? Start with your category and ask two or three acquirers which gateway they support. Then check the plugin table above for that gateway. Install it on staging, run test orders including a refund and a declined card, and only then request the live keys. If a plugin fails any of the five checks, change the plugin before you change the processor. People also ask Is there one best high risk payment gateway for WooCommerce? No. The best choice is the gateway your approved acquirer supports, with a maintained plugin that passes block checkout and HPOS tests. Conclusion A high risk WooCommerce store needs two yeses: one from a merchant account provider, and one from your own checkout. Pick the gateway your acquirer supports, then verify the plugin for block checkout, HPOS and recurring billing on staging. Need a hand? Our team can review your gateway choice and connect it to your store. See our WooCommerce payment gateway integration page to get started. Frequently Asked Questions Do high risk payment gateways work with WooCommerce? Yes, if the gateway has a maintained plugin or an API a developer can integrate. Authorize.Net, NMI, USAePay and CCBill all have WooCommerce plugins. Approval of your business is a separate step with the merchant account provider. Which gateway has an official WooCommerce extension? Authorize.Net is sold on WooCommerce.com at $79 for a 1-year plan. CCBill publishes its own plugin on WordPress.org. The NMI and USAePay plugins we found are by independent developers. Can I use WooPayments or Stripe for a high risk store? Not for many categories. WooPayments lists tobacco and vapes, firearms and ammunition and adult content as prohibited, and Stripe restricts or prohibits several high-risk categories. Check each policy for your exact product. Do these plugins support block checkout and HPOS? Most current listings say yes. Authorize.Net, Gain Commerce NMI, AGMS Pay and the USAePay plugin list HPOS support, and CCBill lists block checkout support. Always test on staging. Where can I see fees and reserve rules for high risk processors? In our high-risk payment processing guide , which compares 15 processors and explains rolling, capped and upfront reserves. Can Virtina connect a high risk gateway to my store? Yes. See our WooCommerce payment gateway integration page for how we review, build and test the checkout.

title: When Should You Redesign Your Ecommerce Website? 10 Warning Signs
headings: Why is your store losing sales when traffic looks fine?
Does your store feel clumsy on a phone?
Are pages slow, and does every fix fade after a month?
Do customers get lost trying to find things?
Is checkout where people give up?
Does your design make first-time visitors trust you less?
Is your platform or tech stack holding the business back?
Are your competitors simply easier to buy from?
Has your brand moved on while your website stayed put?
Is your team afraid to touch the website?
What should you do before you start a redesign?
How do I know if my ecommerce website is outdated?
How often should you redesign an ecommerce website?
Can I fix these problems without a full redesign?
text: Summary Most stores do not need a redesign because the site looks old. They need one because the site stopped doing its job. This guide walks through ten warning signs, from falling conversion and a clumsy mobile experience to slow pages, a leaky checkout, and a platform that no longer fits, and shows how to check each one against your own data. If three or four of them describe your store, it is time to look at a proper ecommerce website redesign before the problem costs more. Introduction Almost every store owner has thought it at some point: maybe we need a new website. It usually arrives after a bad quarter, or after seeing a competitor launch something slick. The trouble is that a redesign is a big decision. It costs money, pulls your team’s attention, and carries real risk if it goes badly. So the useful question is not whether you want a new look. It is whether the current site is holding the business back. Below are ten signs we see again and again in the stores we work with. Each one comes with a quick way to check it, so you can decide with evidence instead of a hunch. Table of Contents Why is your store losing sales when traffic looks fine? Does your store feel clumsy on a phone? Are pages slow, and does every fix fade after a month? Do customers get lost trying to find things? Is checkout where people give up? Does your design make first-time visitors trust you less? Is your platform or tech stack holding the business back? Are your competitors simply easier to buy from? Has your brand moved on while your website stayed put? Is your team afraid to touch the website? What should you do before you start a redesign? People also ask Conclusion Frequently asked questions Why is your store losing sales when traffic looks fine? This is usually the first sign, and the one owners explain away the longest. Visitors still show up and the ad budget has not changed, but fewer of them buy. Nobody can point to one clear reason, so everyone blames the season or the market. When traffic holds and conversion slips over a few quarters, the site itself is the quiet suspect. Product pages that skip the questions buyers actually ask, filters that return nothing useful, and a checkout that feels like paperwork rarely show up as a single alarming number. Together they cost real money. Our guide to ecommerce user experience shows where shoppers tend to get stuck. How to check it Conversion trend. Compare conversion rate over the last four to six quarters, not just month over month. Page-level exits. Look in GA4 for product and cart pages where people leave most often. Does your store feel clumsy on a phone? Open your own store on a phone, on mobile data, and try to buy something. Do not zoom in. If you squint, mis-tap a button, or wait on a slow image, your customers are doing the same thing, and most of them will not push through. A site that was “made responsive” years ago by squeezing a desktop layout into a narrow screen is not the same as one designed for thumbs. When a big share of your visitors are on mobile and they convert far below desktop users, that gap is telling you something. How to check it Device split. Compare conversion rate and revenue per session for mobile and desktop in GA4. Real purchase test. Place a test order on a mid-range phone and note every moment of friction. Are pages slow, and does every fix fade after a month? Every store has a slow page now and then. The warning sign is when you compress images, remove a plugin, upgrade hosting, and the scores creep back down a few weeks later. That pattern usually points to the foundation: a heavy theme, years of stacked scripts, or code nobody wants to touch. Speed also feeds into how Google measures page experience. If you want to understand what a rebuild can change, read why you might hire a Core Web Vitals developer . How to check it Field data. Use the Core Web Vitals report in Search Console, which reflects real visitors, not lab tests. Script audit. List every third-party script and app, and ask which ones still earn their weight. Do customers get lost trying to find things? Watch someone who has never seen your store try to find a specific product. Do they use the menu, or jump to search because the menu did not help? Do they hit dead ends or categories that overlap? Navigation rots slowly. Every new product line adds another menu item until the structure mirrors your internal history instead of how shoppers think. Support emails asking “do you carry…?” about products you obviously carry are a giveaway. How to check it Site search terms. Review what people search for and how many searches return no results. Five-person test. Ask five people outside your team to find three products and watch where they stall. Is checkout where people give up? Look at your funnel. If plenty of people add to cart but a big chunk disappears before payment, checkout is leaking. Forced account creation, surprise shipping costs, too many fields, limited payment options, and error messages that do not say what went wrong are the usual causes. Some of this can be patched. But when checkout is tangled up with an old platform or heavy customizations, each patch gets pricier, and that is often the point where a redesign makes more financial sense than another fix. How to check it Funnel drop-off. Compare cart, shipping, and payment step completion rates in GA4. Field count. Count every required field and remove what you do not truly need. Does your design make first-time visitors trust you less? People decide quickly whether a store looks legitimate. Dated styling, mismatched fonts, blurry product photos, broken icons, and a footer stuck in 2016 all send the same message: nobody is paying attention here. For a first-time buyer spending real money, that doubt is enough to leave. Trust signals matter as much as looks. Clear returns information, visible contact details, genuine reviews, and secure checkout cues should be easy to find, not buried three clicks deep. How to check it New vs returning. Compare conversion for new and returning visitors. A big gap often points to trust. Policy visibility. Make sure shipping, returns, and contact details show on product pages and in the cart. Is your platform or tech stack holding the business back? Sometimes the design is only the symptom. Maybe the platform cannot handle the pricing rules, B2B accounts, integrations, or catalog size you need now. Maybe every small change needs a developer and a week of waiting. Maybe the software is so far out of date that updating it feels risky. If this sounds familiar, the real question is whether you need a facelift or a deeper rebuild. We break that decision down in how to redesign your ecommerce website . How to check it Wish list. Write down the five features you want but cannot build on your current platform. Update risk. Note how long it has been since the core platform and plugins were safely updated. Are your competitors simply easier to buy from? Spend twenty minutes buying from the two or three competitors your customers compare you with. Note what feels easier: search, filters, product comparison, delivery details, reorders, quote requests. If they win on most of it, they are quietly training your customers to expect more than you offer. You do not need to copy anyone. You do need to know where the bar sits. Has your brand moved on while your website stayed put? Businesses change. New product lines, a different customer base, sharper positioning, a rebrand. If the site still speaks for the company you were five years ago, it works against you. Mixed messages between your sales team, your packaging, and your homepage confuse buyers, and confused buyers rarely convert. Is your team afraid to touch the website? This one is easy to miss. If swapping a banner, adding a landing page, or launching a promotion is stressful, slow, or needs outside help every time, the site is costing you agility. Marketing should move at the speed of the market. When it cannot, good ideas die in a queue. What should you do before you start a redesign? Do not jump to mockups. Write down which of the ten signs apply to you and attach a number to each one: conversion by device, checkout drop-off, page speed, support tickets about the same confusion. That list becomes your brief and keeps the project focused on fixing problems instead of chasing trends. Then protect what already works. Pages that rank and earn traffic should not vanish or change URLs without a plan, which is why we wrote about why ecommerce sites lose rankings after a redesign . Finally, decide whether you need a visual refresh, a structural overhaul, or both. A team that has done this many times can usually tell you after a short review. If you want that second opinion, our ecommerce website redesign team can look at your store and say plainly what we would change. People Also Ask How do I know if my ecommerce website is outdated? Look at results, not looks. Falling conversion, a weak mobile experience, slow pages, and a team that struggles to make changes all point to a site that has fallen behind. How often should you redesign an ecommerce website? There is no fixed date. Many stores revisit the site every few years, but the better trigger is performance. Redesign when the data shows the site is holding you back. Can I fix these problems without a full redesign? Sometimes. Slow pages or a clumsy checkout can often be fixed in place. If several signs point to the platform or structure itself, a redesign is usually the cheaper route over time. Conclusion A website does not have to look old to be failing. If sales are slipping, mobile feels awkward, checkout loses people, or your team cannot move quickly, the site is already costing you money, even if nobody has added up the bill. The good news is that every sign here can be measured. Check them honestly and you will know whether you need a few targeted fixes or a real redesign. If you want help making that call, talk to our ecommerce website redesign team or get in touch directly. Frequently Asked Questions How long does an ecommerce redesign usually take? It depends on catalog size, integrations, and how much content needs rework. A focused redesign can take a couple of months, while a large catalog or a platform change takes longer. A good partner gives you a realistic timeline after reviewing your store. Is a redesign the same as a rebuild? No. A redesign changes how the site looks and works for shoppers. A rebuild also changes what runs underneath, such as the platform. Some stores need only the first, others need both. Will a redesign hurt my SEO? It can when URLs change without redirects or page copy gets thinned out. With planning, rankings can be protected. Read how to keep your rankings through a redesign before you start. Can I redesign in phases? Yes. Many stores start with the product page, cart, and checkout because those affect revenue most, then move on to the rest of the site. What should I prepare before talking to a redesign agency? Bring your conversion data, a list of customer complaints, and examples of sites you admire. That gives the team something concrete to scope against.

title: Ecommerce UX Problems That Drive Customers Away
headings: Why do shoppers leave without telling you why?
Can shoppers find what they came for?
Navigation built around your org chart
Does your product page answer the questions shoppers actually have?
What happens when a shopper uses a phone?
Which small details quietly erode trust?
How do you tell which problem is yours?
Is it a quick fix or does it need a redesign?
How does Virtina approach ecommerce UX problems?
text: Summary Most shoppers who leave an online store never tell you why. They just go. This article walks through the ecommerce UX problems behind most of those exits, from search that returns nothing to checkout forms that fight back, and shows how to spot which ones are costing you sales and when fixing them means a redesign. Introduction Nobody emails a store owner to say the filter confused them. They open a competitor’s tab instead. That silence is why UX problems survive for years on stores that otherwise look healthy. Traffic is fine, ads are running, and the numbers never quite add up. This piece covers the problems we see most often when we audit stores, why each one pushes people out, and how to tell a quick fix from a structural issue. If you want the other side of the story, how age and technical debt hold sales back, start with how an outdated ecommerce website hurts conversions . Table of Contents Why do shoppers leave without telling you why? Can shoppers find what they came for? Does your product page answer the questions shoppers actually have? What happens when a shopper uses a phone? Where does checkout lose people? Which small details quietly erode trust? How do you tell which problem is yours? Is it a quick fix or does it need a redesign? How does Virtina approach ecommerce UX problems? Conclusion Frequently asked questions Why do shoppers leave without telling you why? Because leaving is cheaper than complaining. A shopper who hits friction has a dozen alternatives one tab away and no reason to explain themselves. What you see in your analytics is a bounce, an exit page or an abandoned cart. What you never see is the moment of confusion that caused it. That is also why UX problems rarely show up as one dramatic failure. They show up as a pile of small ones. A menu that takes a second guess. A photo that will not zoom. A delivery charge that appears on the very last step. Each one costs you a slice of visitors, and together they decide whether a store converts well or just about gets by. The rest of this article follows the order a shopper meets them: finding products, judging them, using the store on a phone, and paying. Can shoppers find what they came for? Findability is where most stores lose the first round. Two things do the damage: navigation that reflects how your company is organised, and search that cannot cope with the way customers actually type. Navigation built around your org chart Menus often mirror internal departments or supplier names. Shoppers think in jobs and problems, like “something for a small bathroom”, not “Series 400 fixtures”. When category names only make sense to your team, people open three menus, give up on the third and leave. A mega menu with forty links does not fix this. It just hides the problem behind more clicking. Search that returns nothing People who use site search are your most motivated visitors. They already know what they want. If a plural, a typo or a part number sends back “no results”, you have turned away your best prospect at the door. Pull your zero-result search queries and read them. It is one of the quickest ways to learn what customers want that your store is failing to show them. Filters that fight back Filters that reset after every click, hide how many items match, or reload the page and drop the shopper back at the top all feel like work. On a catalogue of a few hundred products, good filtering is the difference between browsing and bouncing. Does your product page answer the questions shoppers actually have? A product page has one job, which is to remove doubt. Plenty of them do the opposite. The usual culprits are a single photo with no zoom and no sense of scale, a description copied word for word from the supplier, and missing basics like sizing, compatibility, materials or delivery time. When shoppers cannot find an answer, they go and look for it somewhere else. Most of them do not come back. B2B stores have their own version of this. No tiered pricing, no spec sheets to download, “call for price” where a number should be, and no simple way to ask for a quote. A buyer comparing three suppliers will not phone to find out what you charge when the other two just tell them. Reviews matter here too. Hidden, buried or missing reviews leave the shopper to judge the product on your word alone, and your word is the least convincing source on the page. What happens when a shopper uses a phone? Most stores are “responsive” in the sense that nothing visibly breaks on a small screen. That is a low bar, and it is not the same as being easy to use. Look for tap targets that are too small for a thumb, a sticky header that swallows a third of the screen, pop-ups with a close button you cannot hit, tables that scroll sideways, and checkout fields that open the wrong keyboard. A page can pass a technical mobile test and still be miserable to shop on. The best test costs nothing. Take a mid-range phone, switch off the Wi-Fi, and try to buy something from your own store. If you feel like giving up halfway through, your customers did a while ago. Where does checkout lose people? Checkout is the one place where UX problems turn straight into lost revenue, because the shopper has already decided to buy. These are the ones we run into most: Forced account creation. Someone who wants to buy one item once does not want a password to remember. Offer guest checkout and invite them to save details afterwards. Surprises at the end. Shipping, handling or tax that only appears on the final step feels like a bait and switch. Show estimates early, on the product page or in the cart. Long, unforgiving forms. Every extra field is a small tax. Remove anything you do not need, support autofill, and put error messages next to the field that caused them instead of in a red banner at the top that sends people hunting. Too few ways to pay. If your customers expect a wallet or a card on file and you only offer one option, some of them will simply stop. No sense of progress. People tolerate a few steps if they know how many are left. A checkout that feels endless gets abandoned. Which small details quietly erode trust? Some problems are not about usability at all. They are about whether the store feels safe to hand money to. A return policy that is hard to find. No phone number or address anywhere. A footer that still says 2019. Broken images, or a page that mixes three visual styles because it has been patched by three different plugins. Newsletter, chat, cookie and discount pop-ups all firing within the first few seconds. Each one is minor on its own. Together they tell the shopper that nobody is looking after the place. Out-of-stock dead ends belong on this list too. A product page that says “sold out” and offers nothing else, no alternative, no back-in-stock alert, gives the shopper nowhere to go but away. And do not skip accessibility. Low-contrast text, missing focus states and menus that cannot be used with a keyboard shut out real customers, and they usually point to deeper problems in how the theme was built. How do you tell which problem is yours? You do not need a research budget. A handful of sources will show you most of what is wrong. Your funnel by device. Look at where visitors drop off on mobile compared with desktop. A big gap at one step usually points at one specific problem. Zero-result searches. Read them. They are a list of things customers wanted and could not find. Session recordings. Watch twenty sessions end to end. Patterns show up faster than you would expect, mostly in the form of people rage-clicking on things that do not respond. Your support inbox. Questions that keep coming back, like “where is my order” or “do you ship to Canada”, are UX bugs in disguise. The answer should have been on the page. Your own phone. Buy something. Time it. Notice every moment you hesitate. If the same problems keep coming back after you fix them, the cause may be deeper than the page. Redesign or rebuild: six calls that decide what your store needs helps you work out which it is. Is it a quick fix or does it need a redesign? Most of the problems above can be fixed in place. Better filters, guest checkout, upfront shipping costs and richer product pages do not need a new website. They need someone to decide to do them. The honest cases for a redesign are the ones where the build itself is in the way. Checkout locked inside a legacy template. Navigation hard-coded into the theme. A mobile layout that has to be rebuilt rather than patched. Every small change needing a developer for a week. A quick test: list the last five UX changes you wanted to make and count how many the platform blocked. If it is most of them, patching will keep costing more than it returns. Budget tends to be the next question, so it helps to know what an ecommerce website redesign costs before you talk to anyone. How does Virtina approach ecommerce UX problems? We start with an audit, not a mock-up. Speed, mobile experience, navigation and checkout get looked at first, because that is where the money is leaking. Anything that can be fixed in place is flagged as a fix. Anything the platform prevents is flagged as a structural issue, so you know whether you are buying a repair or a rebuild. If a redesign is the right call, our ecommerce website redesign service is built around keeping what already works: rankings benchmarked before any change, every old URL redirected and tested, and 30 days of monitoring after launch. Worried about losing traffic along the way? Here is how to protect your rankings through a redesign . Want to see what we would change before committing to anything? Request a free redesign audit and we will show you. Conclusion Customers rarely leave because of one big mistake. They leave because search missed, the product page left a question open, the phone experience was clumsy, or checkout asked for one thing too many. The good news is that most of these are cheap to find and fixable without starting over. Fix what is local first, and be honest about the few problems that come from the build itself. That keeps you from either patching forever or rebuilding before you need to. Frequently Asked Questions What is the biggest ecommerce UX problem? There is no single answer that fits every store. For most, checkout and mobile experience carry the largest losses because they sit closest to the sale. Your own funnel data should decide where to look first. How can I find UX problems without a big budget? Start with funnel drop-off by device, zero-result search queries, a few session recordings, the questions your support team keeps answering, and your own attempt to buy something on a phone. Together they usually surface the main issues in an afternoon. Do UX problems affect SEO? Indirectly, yes. Slow pages, intrusive pop-ups and poor mobile layouts push visitors away, and those engagement problems can feed into how a page performs in search. The bigger SEO risk is usually fixing UX through a redesign without protecting URLs and redirects. How long before UX fixes show results? Small changes such as guest checkout or earlier shipping costs can show up in your data within a few weeks, depending on traffic. Record a baseline before you change anything so you can tell what actually moved. Do I need a full redesign to fix these problems? Usually not. Most UX problems can be fixed in place. A redesign makes sense when the platform or theme blocks the changes you need, or when every fix has become slow and expensive. How often should I review my store UX? A light review every quarter works well for most stores, plus a fresh look after any platform upgrade, theme change or major campaign.

text: Summary Most ecommerce stores that think they need a rebuild actually need a redesign. Six factors, scope, platform limits, technical debt, budget, timeline, and risk tolerance, settle the question almost every time. This article walks through each one as a verdict, not a scorecard. Introduction A redesign that never fixes the real problem just delays the rebuild you actually needed. A rebuild nobody needed burns months and budget on a platform move you could have skipped. Industry conversations often use rebuild and replatform almost interchangeably, and this article does too except where the distinction matters. Six concrete factors decide whether your store needs a redesign or a full rebuild. Each factor below takes a clear side, not a hedge. Table of Contents Scope of change: if the fix lives in templates, call it a redesign Platform constraints: when the platform refuses the feature, call it a rebuild Technical debt: count the patches before you trust the page speed score Budget: a rebuild should run several times a redesign’s cost Timeline: don’t plan a rebuild if you can’t absorb months offline Risk tolerance: a rebuild gambles with revenue you already have What redesign and rebuild actually cost you, side by side What a redesign project involves versus what a rebuild does People also ask Conclusion Frequently asked questions Scope of change: if the fix lives in templates, call it a redesign If you can describe the problem as one page, one flow, or one component, you need a redesign. Scope of change is the first filter, before cost or timeline ever enter the conversation. A confusing checkout flow, an outdated product page, or a broken filter are template-level problems. How to tell a template problem from a platform problem A template problem shows up as a symptom on a specific page or step. A platform problem shows up everywhere a given limitation applies, no matter which template you touch. If a developer could fix it inside the current build, it is scope, not structure. A jewelry retailer once lost sales on one confusing size-selector component, not the whole site. Replacing that single component fixed the problem in two weeks, no platform change required. Platform constraints: when the platform refuses the feature, call it a rebuild The platform forces a rebuild when it structurally cannot support a feature your business needs. Tiered B2B pricing, multi-warehouse inventory, and a checkout step the architecture cannot hold are rebuild signals. No redesign fixes a limitation baked into the platform’s data model or API. Real platform-level limits that force a rebuild Plugin conflicts stacked on an aging theme eventually make every change risky. A SaaS platform’s API ceiling blocks integrations no theme update can work around. An open-source core customized past the point of safely upgrading behaves the same way. Comparing platforms before you commit matters, since a Shopify vs WooCommerce comparison clarifies which constraints you inherit. B2B sellers hit platform ceilings fastest, since complex pricing and account-based catalogs expose limits early. That is why B2B ecommerce development work often starts with an audit of what the platform can and cannot hold. Technical debt: count the patches before you trust the page speed score Technical debt matters more than how the site looks or scores on a speed test. The number of workarounds currently propping up the store predicts the next six months better than any score. A clean speed score can sit on top of a fragile, patched build. What counts as technical debt on an ecommerce store Plugin bloat is the most visible form, where each new plugin quietly conflicts with three others already installed. Duct-taped integrations, undocumented custom code, and abandoned A/B test remnants add weight nobody tracks. Each layer makes the next legitimate change slower and riskier to ship. Look at your last ten store changes. Count how many needed a developer just to avoid breaking something else. If most of them did, technical debt, not design age, is the real constraint. That same patch list raises migration risk later, since nobody fully remembers how the pieces fit together. A staging environment eventually stops catching every regression before launch. Budget: a rebuild should run several times a redesign’s cost Treat rebuild cost as a multiple of redesign cost, never as a close number. If a quoted rebuild costs about the same as a redesign, something in the scope is being underpriced. A full platform migration touches data, integrations, and testing a template refresh never does. Why a close quote is a warning sign A rebuild quote close to a redesign quote usually means scope was cut somewhere, not that the project got cheaper. Missing line items show up later as change orders, which is worse than paying for them upfront. Treat figures here as directional, since no reliable public data sets a fixed cost or project timeline for either path. A detailed ecommerce website cost breakdown is a better starting point than any single vendor quote. Timeline: don’t plan a rebuild if you can’t absorb months offline A redesign fits inside a quarter, while a rebuild rarely does. Pretending otherwise is how rebuild timelines blow past their original deadline. Total cost of ownership should include the months your team spends on the project, not just the invoice. Why timeline pressure is itself a valid reason to choose redesign A business that cannot spare its product or engineering team for half a year has already answered the question. Timeline pressure is not a constraint to work around, it is a legitimate factor on its own. A rebuild that slips its timeline also slips its budget, almost without exception. Risk tolerance: a rebuild gambles with revenue you already have A rebuild puts existing revenue at risk through data loss, downtime, or broken integrations. Migrating a working store is not neutral, it risks GMV you are already earning. Only accept that migration risk once the current platform is already costing more than the risk itself. When the other five factors point here Scope, platform limits, technical debt, budget, and timeline all funnel into this one question: is the gamble worth it. If the first five factors point toward rebuild, risk tolerance is the final check, not a new argument. If they don’t, risk tolerance alone should stop you from rebuilding. Store owners already weighing platform risk can see owners leaving Shopify for exactly this reason, not because WooCommerce is trendy. Ownership of your own platform is what keeps that risk inside your control. What redesign and rebuild actually cost you, side by side The table below lines up redesign and rebuild across the five factors that matter most. Use it as a sanity check against any quote you receive. It is not a fixed price list for your specific store. Factor Redesign Rebuild / replatform Cost Typically around 1x baseline (illustrative) Typically 3x to 5x baseline (illustrative) Timeline Weeks to about 3 months 4 to 8+ months Risk to existing revenue Low, contained to specific pages or flows Real risk: data loss, downtime, broken integrations possible What you keep Platform, data model, integrations, most SEO equity A clean slate, free of legacy codebase limits What you lose Legacy platform-level constraints stay in place Platform familiarity, plus integration work that must be redone Figures are directional, industry-typical ranges for illustration only, not sourced statistics, as of October 2026. What a redesign project involves versus what a rebuild does A redesign moves through design and template phases, while a rebuild adds a full platform migration on top. The two projects share a goal, a better-performing store, but almost no phases in common. A full rebuild sometimes also means moving toward headless commerce, which is a bigger architecture change than either path alone. Inside a redesign project A redesign starts with an audit of the current build, then moves into UX and visual direction. Template-level development follows, then QA against your existing URLs and SEO equity, then a staged rollout. The deliverable is new templates, not a new data model. A typical team is a designer, a front-end developer, and QA, with no data migration specialist required. One factual note worth planting here: an ecommerce website redesign project is exactly this scope, not a platform swap. Inside a rebuild or replatform project A rebuild starts with platform selection, then a full data migration plan. Integration rebuilds for ERP, PIM, payment, and 3PL systems follow, alongside redirect mapping for SEO. Parallel QA on the new platform and a defined cutover window close out the project. The deliverable is a new platform instance, not just new templates. A typical team adds a migration and integration specialist, plus a longer QA and staging cycle. A documented WooCommerce migration guide is a useful reference for what that staging cycle actually involves. Whichever path fits, the team executing it matters as much as the decision itself. Teams offering WooCommerce development services with both template and migration specialists can run either project well. People also ask Is replatforming the same thing as a rebuild? Not exactly, though the terms are often used interchangeably. Replatforming usually means moving to a new platform while keeping most business logic intact. In practice, the two terms blur together once a project actually starts. How do I know if my ecommerce site needs a redesign or a rebuild? Run the six factors above against your own store: scope, platform constraints, technical debt, budget, timeline, and risk tolerance. If most point toward redesign, trust that result instead of defaulting to the bigger project. A rebuild is the exception, not the default. Can I redesign my site without losing SEO rankings? Yes, if the redesign is scoped around preserving URLs, redirects, and existing content, not just the visual layer. SEO risk comes from sloppy migration work, not from the act of redesigning itself. Treat redirect mapping and QA as mandatory steps, not optional ones. What’s the difference between a website refresh and a full redesign? A refresh changes colors, fonts, and imagery without touching how the store functions. A full redesign changes layout, navigation, and checkout flow to fix how shoppers actually move through the store. Scope of change separates the two, not how different the final result looks. Conclusion Six factors decide this question far better than a feeling about how old the site looks. Scope, platform limits, technical debt, budget, timeline, and risk tolerance each point in one direction. Most stores land on redesign once they run through all six honestly. Save the rebuild for the rare case where the platform itself is the real blocker. Frequently Asked Questions What’s the difference between redesign and replatform? A redesign changes the templates and experience on your current platform. A replatform moves the store to a new platform entirely, including its data model and integrations. The two terms are often used loosely, but that distinction is the one that actually matters for scoping a project. How long does an ecommerce rebuild take? A rebuild typically runs four to eight months or more, depending on catalog size and integration count. A redesign usually fits inside a quarter by comparison. Treat both as directional ranges, not fixed quotes, since every store’s scope differs. Is a rebuild worth it for a smaller store? Store size matters less than whether the platform is actually blocking you. A small store hitting a genuine platform ceiling still needs a rebuild. A larger store with only template-level problems still only needs a redesign. Do I lose my SEO rankings in a rebuild? You risk losing rankings if redirects, URL structure, and content aren’t carried over deliberately. A rebuild does not have to cost rankings if migration QA treats SEO as a first-class requirement. Most ranking losses trace back to skipped redirect mapping, not the platform change itself. What does technical debt actually look like day to day? It looks like every small change needing a developer because the last five patches made the build fragile. It shows up as plugins nobody remembers installing and integrations held together with undocumented custom code. The warning sign is the pattern, not any single incident. Should I redesign before or after fixing a slow site? Fix the slow site first if speed is a local, fixable problem on the current platform. Fold speed work into the redesign itself if slow pages are one symptom among several. Either way, do not approve a new design without a measurable speed target attached. What’s the biggest mistake businesses make in this decision? The biggest mistake is skipping straight to a rebuild because the site feels old. Nobody checks first whether the problem is actually structural. The second most common mistake is choosing a platform based on a vendor’s preference instead of your own constraints. How do I estimate rebuild cost before getting a quote? Start with the comparison table above and treat the multiples as a baseline, not a final number. Multiply your last redesign cost, or a reasonable market estimate for one, by three to five. Use that range to sanity-check any vendor quote you receive.

text: Summary An ecommerce website redesign usually costs $3,000 to $12,000 for a small store, $10,000 to $40,000 for a mid-market store, and $50,000 to $200,000 or more for a large B2B or enterprise build. The price follows scope: catalog size, integrations, custom features and platform. This article shows what drives the number, which costs are easy to miss, and how to set a budget before you ask for quotes. Introduction Ask three agencies what a redesign costs and you may get three very different numbers. That is not always padding. The quotes often cover different things: one includes redirects, testing and training, another leaves them out. A store with 200 products and a standard checkout is a different project from one with 20,000 SKUs, an ERP connection and customer-specific pricing. This guide gives realistic ranges by project type, explains what pushes the price up, and shows how to judge cost against return. If you are still deciding whether to redesign at all, start with how an outdated store hurts conversions . Table of Contents How much does an ecommerce website redesign cost? What drives the cost of an ecommerce redesign? What costs are missing from the first quote? How long does a redesign take, and how should you budget? How can you control redesign cost without cutting corners? How Virtina prices a redesign People also ask Conclusion Frequently asked questions How much does an ecommerce website redesign cost? Most redesigns fall into five bands, and the band you land in depends on how much of the store has to change underneath the design. The table below places your project. These are industry ranges compiled from published 2026 pricing guides, not Virtina quotes, so use them to orient yourself rather than to price a job. Project type Typical range (USD) Typical timeline Best fit Theme or template refresh $350 to $8,000 1 to 6 weeks Small catalog, standard checkout, mostly cosmetic goals Freelancer or small-team custom redesign $3,000 to $12,000 4 to 8 weeks Growing store that needs new layouts and a better product page Agency redesign, same platform $10,000 to $40,000 6 to 12 weeks Established store with real traffic, custom features and conversion goals Replatform plus redesign $10,000 to $50,000+ 8 to 20 weeks Moving between Shopify, WooCommerce, Magento or BigCommerce while redesigning Enterprise or complex B2B rebuild $50,000 to $200,000+ 12 weeks to 12 months Large catalogs, ERP, punchout, tiered pricing, multiple storefronts What do the bands mean in practice? Refresh. A new theme on the same structure. Fast and cheap, but it does not fix checkout, search or data problems. Custom redesign. New layouts, new product and category templates, and a reworked checkout, built on the platform you already use. Replatform plus redesign. The design work plus a full data migration, which is where most budgets stretch. Enterprise or B2B rebuild. Business logic, integrations and account features dominate the cost, not the visual design. How does the platform change the price? On Shopify, published guides put template-based work at $3,000 to $12,000, mid-market custom builds at $12,000 to $40,000, and Shopify Plus or complex migrations at $40,000 to $150,000 or more. For WooCommerce, freelancer-led redesigns typically run $3,000 to $12,000, and agency work follows the mid-market and enterprise bands above. Published ranges for Magento (Adobe Commerce) are scarce. These projects tend to land in the upper rows because of larger catalogs and heavier integrations. Our Shopify vs WooCommerce comparison covers running costs, which matter as much as the build price. If you are planning a new store rather than a redesign, see how to calculate the cost of building an ecommerce website . What drives the cost of an ecommerce redesign? Six factors explain most of the gap between a $10,000 quote and a $100,000 one. Knowing them lets you tell an agency what is in scope before it prices the work. Catalog size and data complexity Moving 500 products with variants and attributes takes far more care than moving 50. Every product, category and image has to land on the right page with the right data. Design depth A modified theme costs a fraction of a custom design built from research, wireframes and tested layouts. Custom work also needs more rounds of review. Integrations Every connection to an ERP, CRM, inventory system, shipping tool or payment gateway has to be rebuilt or re-tested on the new store. Industry guides put typical stores at 5 to 15 connected apps, and each one adds scope. B2B and custom functionality Quoting and RFQ flows, customer-specific pricing, punchout, account hierarchies and approval workflows are custom work on most platforms. They are the main reason B2B redesigns sit in the top rows of the table. Content and media New product photography, rewritten copy and new category pages add real cost when existing assets are not good enough to carry over. Protecting your search traffic Redirect maps, structured data and launch checks usually cost a few thousand dollars on an ecommerce site, which is small next to a ranking drop. We cover the details in why ecommerce sites lose rankings after a redesign . What costs are missing from the first quote? Published pricing guides estimate that overlooked items add 15 to 25 percent to the initial quote. Ask every agency whether these are included or billed separately, so you can compare quotes line by line. Often missed Typical cost (USD) Staging and testing environments $500 to $2,000 Performance optimisation $500 to $2,000 Email template updates (order, shipping, account) $300 to $1,500 Accessibility compliance work $2,000 to $8,000 Professional product photography $3,000 to $15,000 Content migration, per page $75 to $150 Team training on the new admin $200 to $800 per session Post-launch support retainer $500 to $2,500 per month What changes in the running costs after launch? Platform and app subscriptions, and hosting, continue after the build is paid for. A cheaper build on a platform with high monthly fees can cost more over three years than a pricier build on one with low fees. Compare total cost over three years, not the build price alone. How long does a redesign take, and how should you budget? Most standard redesigns take 8 to 12 weeks from audit to launch. Larger B2B stores with ERP integrations usually take 12 to 16 weeks. A timeline that stretches usually costs more, because the team is billed for the extra time. How do you judge cost against return? A redesign pays for itself when the added revenue is larger than the total cost. As an illustration only, a store earning $1,000,000 a year whose conversion rate rises from 1.5 percent to 1.8 percent at the same traffic gains about $200,000 a year. Your numbers will differ, so use your own revenue, traffic and conversion rate. How do you set a ceiling before asking for quotes? Estimate the added revenue over 12 to 24 months using the lowest lift you can defend, then subtract the running costs. What remains is the most the project can cost and still make sense. Share the ceiling and the scope with each agency so the quotes are comparable. How can you control redesign cost without cutting corners? Five habits keep a redesign on budget without trading away the parts that protect revenue. Start with an audit. You pay to fix what is actually costing sales rather than redoing everything. Keep the platform unless it is the real problem. Replatforming is the largest single cost multiplier. Prepare content and product data before kickoff. Late copy and photography are a common cause of overruns. Agree scope in writing. Put new ideas on a phase two list, not into the current build. Launch in phases if the budget is tight. Do the templates that drive revenue first (home, category, product page, cart, checkout) and secondary pages later. The cheapest quote is rarely the lowest cost. A redesign that skips testing, redirects or performance work often needs a paid fix within months, and that fix tends to cost more than doing it properly the first time. How Virtina prices a redesign We do not publish fixed prices, because two stores with the same page count can have very different integrations and data. We start with a free redesign audit, then give a fixed quote for the agreed scope. If you want a rough number first, try our ecommerce cost calculator . To see what happens at each stage, read our five-step redesign process , or review our ecommerce website redesign services . People also ask Is a redesign cheaper than a rebuild? Usually yes, when the platform and data stay the same. A rebuild or replatform adds migration, testing and integration work, which is why those projects sit in the higher rows of the table. Why do agency quotes for the same store differ so much? Quotes differ in scope, not just price. One may include redirects, testing, accessibility and training while another leaves them out, so compare line by line. Is a template redesign good enough? It can be, for a small catalog with a standard checkout. It will not fix slow pages, weak search or a checkout that loses orders, because those sit below the theme. Conclusion An ecommerce redesign can cost a few thousand dollars or well into six figures. The difference comes from catalog size, integrations, custom features and platform, not from how polished the design looks. Set a ceiling from the revenue you expect to gain, ask every agency to quote the same scope, and check what each quote leaves out. That keeps the budget honest from the first conversation. Frequently Asked Questions How much does it cost to redesign a small ecommerce website? Most small stores land between $3,000 and $12,000, depending on whether they use a template or a custom design and how many products and integrations they have. How long does an ecommerce redesign take? Standard projects take 8 to 12 weeks, and larger B2B stores with ERP connections take 12 to 16 weeks. What should a redesign quote include? At minimum: design, development, data migration, redirects, testing, performance work, training and a launch plan. If any of these are missing, ask whether they are billed separately. Can I spread the cost by redesigning in phases? Yes. Launch the pages that drive revenue first (home, category, product, cart and checkout) and schedule secondary pages for a later phase. Will a redesign hurt my SEO? It can if URLs, titles and structured data are not carried over. Plan for it from the start with our guide to keeping rankings through a redesign . Virtina builds and rebuilds stores on WooCommerce, Magento, BigCommerce and Shopify. Tell us about your store and we will review it, point out what is costing you sales and give you a fixed quote. text: Summary Magento 2.4.6 lost regular support on August 11, 2026. If you run Magento Open Source, there is no extended patch window to fall back on, so you need a plan. The choice is to upgrade to a supported 2.4.x release or move to another platform, and the right answer depends on how much custom logic your store carries. This guide explains each date, the risks, the options, rough costs, and a 30-day plan. Introduction Many store owners learned about this date from a plugin vendor email or a developer, not from Adobe. If that was you, the practical questions are simple. Am I affected, how urgent is it, and should I upgrade or leave Magento? This guide answers those questions in plain language and gives you a rough sense of cost and time. It is a decision guide, not a technical manual, and it is written for store owners and marketing and operations leads who need to brief a developer or agency. By the end, you will know your dates, your options, and what to do this month. Table of Contents Summary Introduction Who is affected by the Magento 2.4.6 end of support? What does each Magento support date mean for your store? What actually changes now that regular support has ended? Does running an unsupported Magento version put your PCI compliance at risk? Does Magento Open Source get extended patches like Adobe Commerce does? How do PHP and server requirements affect your upgrade timeline? Should you upgrade Magento or move to another platform? How do your options compare side by side? How much do a Magento upgrade and a migration cost, and how long do they take? What drives upgrade effort more than anything else? How do you protect your SEO if you leave Magento? What mistakes should you avoid while deciding? What should you do in the next 30 days? People also ask Conclusion Frequently asked questions Who is affected by the Magento 2.4.6 end of support? Any store running Magento Open Source 2.4.6 or older is affected. Regular support for 2.4.6 ended on August 11, 2026, which means you are no longer on a version that Adobe actively maintains in its regular release cycle. If you pay for Adobe Commerce, your position is softer, because Adobe Commerce customers get an extended support window for 2.4.6. If you run the free Open Source edition, which is what most mid-size Magento stores use, there is no equivalent safety net. The quick test takes one minute. Log in to your Magento admin and read the version number in the footer. If it starts with 2.4.6 or lower, this guide is written for you. If you are on 2.4.7 or newer, you are covered for now, but your own deadline is closer than it looks, and the next section explains why. It also helps to know who else should care. Agencies maintaining client stores, ERP and shipping integrators, and extension vendors are all moving their test matrices to newer versions. Even if your store looks fine today, the ecosystem around it is already shifting. What does each Magento support date mean for your store? Support dates sound abstract until you translate them into risk. Here is the plain version, using the dates Adobe has published for the 2.4 line. Version Regular support ends What it means for you 2.4.6 Aug 11, 2026 (passed) No more regular releases. You are running on a version Adobe no longer maintains in the regular cycle. 2.4.7 May 31, 2027 About eight months of regular support left. A short runway, not a destination. 2.4.8 May 31, 2028 About 19 months of runway from today. 2.4.9 May 31, 2029 The longest runway. Released in May 2026. Regular support means Adobe ships fixes and security patches for that version. Once it ends, new vulnerabilities in Magento core or its dependencies may not be patched for your version. Third-party extension vendors also tend to stop testing against it, and some quietly drop it from their compatibility lists. Notice the pattern in the table. Each new release gives you roughly three years of runway, but 2.4.7 has only about eight months left. If you are planning an upgrade, jumping straight to 2.4.8 or 2.4.9 usually makes more sense than landing on a version that expires next spring. What actually changes now that regular support has ended? Nothing breaks on the day support ends. Your store keeps taking orders, your admin keeps loading, and your customers notice nothing. That is exactly why this deadline is easy to ignore, and why it is risky. What changes is the slow accumulation of exposure. Security researchers keep finding issues in PHP, in server software, and in libraries Magento depends on. On a supported version, the fixes arrive in a patch. On an unsupported one, you either backport them yourself or you accept the gap. Extensions are the second pressure point. Payment gateways, shipping carriers, tax tools, and ERP connectors update their own APIs regularly. Their developers test against current versions first, so an old store finds that new releases of its extensions need newer Magento, and old releases of its extensions slowly go stale. The third pressure point is people. Developers who know the newest Magento releases are easier to hire than those who want to keep nursing an old one, and agencies price legacy maintenance accordingly. Waiting rarely makes the work cheaper. Does running an unsupported Magento version put your PCI compliance at risk? It can. Payment card rules expect the software that touches card data to be supported and kept up to date with vendor security patches. An unsupported platform is a common finding when an auditor or acquiring bank reviews a merchant. How strictly that applies to you depends on how you take payments. A store that sends shoppers to a hosted payment page has a smaller scope than a store that handles card data on its own checkout. Your acquiring bank or your assessor decides what is acceptable, not your developer and not Adobe. The safest move is to ask them directly. Tell your payment provider or compliance contact which Magento version you run and when you plan to upgrade, and get their position in writing. That conversation is far cheaper before an audit than during one. We are not your assessor, and this section is general information rather than compliance advice. For the broader picture of PCI and the four paths available to you, our earlier guide goes deeper: The August 2026 Magento Support Cliff . Does Magento Open Source get extended patches like Adobe Commerce does? According to the lifecycle summaries we reviewed, extended support after the regular window is an Adobe Commerce benefit, not an Open Source one. For 2.4.6, that extended window is reported to run to late August 2027, with security-only coverage after that. For Open Source owners, that means the regular end date is the date that matters. Treat the extended dates as a reference for Adobe Commerce customers, and confirm the exact terms for your licence directly in Adobe’s lifecycle policy before you plan around them. This is also why the dates can look more generous online than they feel in practice. A date that reads “extended to 2028” on a blog post may not apply to the edition you actually run. Always check the edition before you trust the date. How do PHP and server requirements affect your upgrade timeline? Magento versions are tied to specific PHP, database, and search engine versions, and those have their own end-of-life dates. PHP 8.2 security support ends on December 31, 2026, so a store stuck on an older PHP release is exposed from two directions at once. Newer Magento releases also expect newer infrastructure. For example, Magento 2.4.8 targets PHP 8.4 or 8.3, and 2.4.9 targets PHP 8.5, along with MySQL 8.4 or a recent MariaDB release. Upgrading Magento therefore often means upgrading your hosting stack at the same time, which affects both cost and testing. This is one of the most overlooked line items in upgrade quotes. Ask whoever estimates your upgrade whether the price includes server changes, a staging environment, and performance testing on the new stack. A quote that covers only the Magento files is incomplete. Should you upgrade Magento or move to another platform? This is the real decision, and it is rarely about the end date itself. The end date is just the moment that forces the question. When staying on Magento and upgrading makes sense Upgrade when your store depends on things Magento does well. That usually means complex catalogs with many attributes, custom pricing rules, customer-group pricing, deep ERP or warehouse integrations, or B2B logic that you have already built and paid for. Moving those features to a new platform means rebuilding them, and that is where migration budgets balloon. When moving to another platform makes sense Move when your Magento store is expensive to maintain, slow to change, and mostly sells a simple catalog. In that case, an upgrade just renews a cost you were already unhappy with. Shopify suits simpler catalogs and teams that want less infrastructure, BigCommerce handles larger catalogs well, and WooCommerce suits teams that want control and a WordPress content engine. See our Magento migration services page for how we scope either route, and our WooCommerce migration and Shopify migration pages if you already know where you are heading. A useful tie-breaker If you were already planning a redesign or a replatform in the next 12 months, do it now instead of paying for an upgrade you will throw away. Our guide on redesign or rebuild walks through the six calls that decide which one your store needs. How do your options compare side by side? There are more than two doors here, and the right one depends on your catalog, your team, and your budget. This table summarizes the main paths. Path Best fit Trade-off Upgrade to 2.4.8 or 2.4.9 Stores with custom pricing, ERP links, B2B rules, or a large extension set Keeps your logic intact, but you keep paying to maintain Magento Adobe Commerce (paid) Larger merchants who need B2B depth and vendor-backed support Licence and hosting costs are significantly higher Community fork such as Mage-OS Technical teams that want to keep their Magento investment and stay on a patched code line Community-driven, so you need a partner who knows it well Replatform to Shopify or BigCommerce Simpler catalogs and teams that want less infrastructure to run Rebuilds custom logic, so complexity raises the bill Replatform to WooCommerce Content-led brands and teams that want full control and a WordPress engine Needs careful planning for large catalogs and B2B rules No path is universally best. The worst choice is the one made by default, which is usually “do nothing until something breaks”. How much do a Magento upgrade and a migration cost, and how long do they take? Real quotes depend on a technical audit, so treat everything here as directional, industry-typical ranges rather than a Virtina price list. The figures below come from a published 2026 industry guide and are meant to give you a sense of scale. Upgrading to a supported 2.4.x release: published ranges run from a few thousand dollars for a lightly customized store to six figures for a heavily customized one, and typically take one to four months. Extension compatibility and custom code drive most of the variance. Adobe Commerce: published estimates start in the tens of thousands of dollars per year for the licence alone, before implementation and hosting. It makes sense mainly for merchants whose B2B or enterprise needs justify it. Replatforming: published ranges for a move to Shopify Plus or BigCommerce commonly start in the tens of thousands of dollars and run well past that for complex catalogs. Timelines of four to nine months are common once data migration, redirects, and testing are included. The cheapest option is not always the one with the lowest invoice. An upgrade is cheaper today, but a platform you keep paying to patch can cost more over three years. Ask every vendor for a quote split into discovery, core work, infrastructure, extensions, integrations, testing, and SEO migration, so you can compare like with like. What drives upgrade effort more than anything else? Surprisingly, it is not Magento core. Core upgrades are well documented. The effort comes from everything you added on top of it. Extensions: every third-party module needs a compatible release for your target version. Some are abandoned, and replacing them is real work. Custom code: overrides, plugins, and custom modules written years ago may rely on behavior that has changed. Theme: older themes often need rework for newer versions and for current performance expectations. Integrations: ERP, shipping, tax, and payment connections all need regression testing. The fastest way to get an honest estimate is an audit that lists every extension and custom module, marks which have a compatible version, and flags what must be rebuilt. Without that list, any quote is a guess. How do you protect your SEO if you leave Magento? A platform move is one of the riskiest moments for organic traffic, but the risk is manageable when it is planned. Most ranking losses after a migration come from a few avoidable mistakes. Map every URL that earns traffic or links, and set up one-to-one 301 redirects before launch. Keep page titles, headings, and body content intact on the pages that rank. Preserve structured data, canonical tags, and your XML sitemap, then submit the new sitemap on launch day. Finally, monitor rankings, crawl errors, and indexed pages daily for the first few weeks. If you stay on Magento and only upgrade, SEO risk is much lower, because your URLs and content do not change. That is one more reason an upgrade can be the lower-risk route for stores that already rank well. What mistakes should you avoid while deciding? Three mistakes show up again and again. The first is waiting for a security scare before acting, because emergency work costs more and gets rushed. The second is choosing a platform based on a competitor or a sales pitch instead of your own catalog and team. The third is skipping the audit, then discovering halfway through that a key extension has no compatible version. A fourth, quieter mistake is treating an upgrade as a pure technical task. It is also a chance to remove extensions you no longer use, clean up your catalog, and fix the speed problems your customers have been quietly putting up with. What should you do in the next 30 days? You do not need to decide everything this week, but you should not leave it open either. A sensible order looks like this. Week 1: confirm your exact Magento version, PHP version, and edition. Tell your payment provider or compliance contact where you stand. Week 2: list every extension and custom module, and check which have releases for 2.4.8 or 2.4.9. Week 3: run a technical audit and collect two estimates: one for upgrading and one for migrating. Week 4: decide with numbers in front of you, and put a start date on the decision. If you would like a second opinion, talk to our Magento team and we will tell you plainly whether upgrading or moving fits your store. People also ask Is Magento 2.4.6 still supported? Regular support ended on August 11, 2026. Adobe Commerce customers have an extended window, but Open Source does not. Which Magento version is supported now? 2.4.7, 2.4.8, and 2.4.9 are within regular support, ending May 2027, May 2028, and May 2029 respectively. Can I stay on Magento 2.4.6? You can, but you carry the security and compatibility risk yourself, and your payment or compliance contact may have a view. Is Magento Open Source being discontinued? What ended is the support window for older versions, not the product itself. Check Adobe’s current announcements for the latest position. Is it cheaper to upgrade or to migrate? Upgrades are usually cheaper up front. Migration can win over several years when your Magento maintenance costs are high. Conclusion Magento 2.4.6 is out of regular support, and Open Source stores do not get an extended window to hide behind. The date does not force a panic, but it does force a decision. Upgrade if your store depends on custom logic and integrations that are costly to rebuild. Move if your Magento build is costly to maintain and your catalog is simple. Either way, ask your payment contact where they stand, get an audit, get numbers, and set a date. If you want help weighing it, our Magento migration services team is happy to review your store. Frequently Asked Questions Is my Magento 2.4.6 store going to stop working? No. Your store keeps running. What changes is that new security issues may go unpatched for your version, and extensions and integrations gradually stop supporting it. Is it safe to stay on 2.4.6 for another year? It is a risk you should accept deliberately, not by default. Payment card rules expect timely security patches, so check with your payment provider or compliance contact before you decide to wait. Which version should I upgrade to? Most stores target the newest release that their extensions and hosting support. 2.4.9 has the longest support runway, while 2.4.8 is a common stepping stone if an extension is not ready yet. How long does a Magento upgrade take? A lightly customized store can often be done in a few weeks. Heavily customized stores, or stores with many extensions, can take a few months once testing is included. Can I skip versions and upgrade straight to the latest? Usually yes, but each jump needs its extensions and PHP stack to be compatible. An audit tells you whether a direct jump is safe or whether you need a staged path. Will moving off Magento hurt my SEO? It can if redirects, URLs, and metadata are not planned. A well-run migration maps every important URL, keeps content intact, and monitors rankings after launch. Do I need Adobe Commerce to stay supported? Not necessarily. Upgrading Open Source to a supported 2.4.x release keeps you inside regular support. Adobe Commerce adds extended support and extra features, at a higher cost. What is the first thing I should do this week? Confirm your exact Magento and PHP versions, then ask a developer for an extension and custom code audit. Everything else, including the upgrade or migrate decision, depends on that list.
